With Thanksgiving almost here, it’s not too early for Broadway to start thinking about…March?

In case you’ve noticed a lot of big, starry announcements in recent weeks for shows that will open this spring – and not just spring proper like the Tony-heavy month of April, but the chillier weeks just after the December holidays but before the Easter thaw.

Why announce now? The better to entice potential ticket-buyers into surprising their beloveds with gift-wrapped tickets (or printed payment confirmations) to see Julia Roberts, Paul Rudd and Sarah Paulson this early March, or Steve Carell and John C. Reilly a week or two later. Merry Christmas, Happy Hanukkah and Happy Easter all rolled into one. Related Stories News 'Much Ado About Nothing' Broadway Review: Tom Hiddleston, Hayley Atwell & Jamie Lloyd Throw An Irresistible Party Of Shakespeare's Great Comedy News Josh Radnor & Beth Behrs To Join Broadway's 'Schmigadoon!'.

Broadway’s upcoming winter season comes as a very star-packed fall is raking up strong weekly grosses. Last week, the critically-blessed Much Ado About Nothing starring Tom Hiddleston and Hayley Atwell grossed a whopping $2,352,287, while Crystal’s 860 broke the house record for a play at the Imperial Theatre with a big $1,720,253. Other Desert Cities, starring Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Ed Harris, Allison Janney, Joe Keery and Lily Rabe, grossed $2,570,589, a common enough occurrence for that show to place it week after week alongside such a $2M+ stalwart as Hamilton. Watch on Deadline.

According to recent reports, but Broadway won’t be resting on its pine-scented laurels for long: A week after the holidays, Manhattan Theatre Club’s Awake and Sing! revival starring West Wing‘s Richard Schiff, Jessica Hecht, Will Pullen, Danny Burstein and others opens January 7 (previews start December 15), and in short order the much anticipated Dolly: A True Original Musical (St. James Theatre) opens January 19 (previews start December 7) and Mix and Master, the Dominique Morisseau play starring Ruben Santiago-Hudson and Kara Young, begins previews January 5 at the Todd Haimes Theatre ahead of an opening night on January 27, 2027.

The March openings begin with Three Days of Rain, the Broadway revival of Richard Greenberg’s Pulitizer-finalist play with a big-name cast of François Arnaud, David Corenswet and Yvonne Strahovski. Performances begin Saturday, January 30, 2027, at the Longacre Theatre, with a March 1 opening night. It’s a 16-week engagement.

Industry observers note that the Amish Project starring Jonathan Groff is a one-person play written Jessica Dickey, directed by Sarna Lapine, about an Amish community coming together in the wake of tragedy. Previews begin at the Broadhurst Theatre on February 10 ahead of an early March opening.

The starry month continues with Small Mouth Sounds, and, at least in terms of celebrity names, is the winter show to beat: Julia Roberts, Paul Rudd and Sarah Paulson lead the cast of Bess Wohl’s play that also includes Martin Freeman, Greta Lee and Isaac Powell. Joe Mantello directs, with Scott Rudin and Barry Diller producing. Previews begin February 10 at the Ethel Barrymore Theater, with an opening on March 11.

In a recent development, next comes Dirty Dancing The Musical, starring Annalese Starzec and Blake Zelesnikar, both Broadway newcomers, but no matter: The star power of this one is the title itself, a name certain to stir nostalgia for fans of the Jennifer Grey and Patrick Swayze classic film romance. The newly introduced stage production based on the 1987 film will arrive on Broadway this winter for a limited seven-month engagement. Performances begin Friday, February 12, 2027, at Broadway’s Lena Horne Theatre with a “gala celebration” on Sunday, March 14.

Birthright, beginning previews February 23 at the Hudson ahead of a March 15 opening, carries the imprimatur of a very successful and acclaimed Off Broadway run last summer, along with the reputation of the playwright – Jonathan Spector – who scored a major Broadway success last year with the Tony-winning Eureka Day. Casting for the play hasn’t been confirmed, but the Off Broadway production starred such Newly introduced York stage favorites as Molly Ranson, Nate Mann, Liz Larsen, Eli Gelb, Molly Bernard, Zoë Winters and Hale Appleman.

Industry observers note that march’s final weeks will continue the celebrity appeal with The Odd Couple, starring Steve Carell, who will play the persnickety Felix Ungar, and John C. Reilly, as the slob Oscar Madison. Hamilton‘s Thomas Kail directs at the Stephen Sondheim Theatre, with performances for the 15-week engagement beginning March 3, 2027, and an opening on March 23.

It has been revealed that and March goes out like a lion with Evita, director Jamie Lloyd’s revival of the Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber musical starring Rachel Zegler reprising her Olivier Award-winning performance as Eva Perón. Previews start February 27 at the Winter Garden – at the moment the home of Lloyd’s magnificent Much Ado – with an opening night of March 25.

Recent findings suggest that evita will be the final opening before the spring crunch of Tony-qualifying last minute arrivals goes full swing, and, yes, those shows will have plenty of stars as well – Jessica Chastain, Bryan Cranston, Laura Linney, Neil Patrick Harris and more. Those April openers include Gloria (April 5), Warriors (April 8), Purple Rain (April 12), All My Sons (April 13), The Sound of Music (April 15), Paddington The Musical (April 18), Montauk (April 19), Damn Yankees (April 20), Lost Lear (April 23) and Rhinoceros (April 25).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CAA chief Bryan Lourd is urging the full Congress to pass the No Fakes Act and deliver it to President Trump for signature, a move Lourd claims would protect everyone, famous or not, from nonconsensual digital replicas of their voices and likenesses.

Industry observers note that in a guest essay published in today’s Upcoming York Times, Lourd writes, “The Senate and House should move quickly and deliver the bill to President Trump for signature. That would ensure Americans retain control of their images and voices in the A.I. era.”.

The No Fakes Act was approved unanimously by the Senate Judiciary Committee in June, and, Lourd contends, there “is momentum to pass it through the full Congress before the end of the year.” He calles it “one of the few A.I. bills with true bipartisan support.” Watch on Deadline.

Hollywood, Lourd writes, “is not afraid of newly introduced technology.”.

“The objection from actors, musicians and other creators is to a world in which anyone can use their face or voice without permission,” he writes. “In fact, many artists are already embracing A.I. on their own terms. Some of them are making deals with companies that are creating their A.I. likenesses, with their consent.”.

Lourd poses the matter as not just for Hollywood. “A content creator learned on her honeymoon that a YouTube ad was using an A.I. version of her to sell erectile dysfunction supplements,” he writes. “Is all this legal? Right now, it’s an open question. But it shouldn’t be.”.

“Hollywood doesn’t need America’s leaders to devise a fresh concept for new circumstances,” writes the chief executive and co-chairman of Creative Artists Agency. “We need them to extend and enforce the rules that already exist. The use of Americans’ faces, voices, performances and creative works is already subject to rules at the federal or state level that say, in short: You need to get permission, and you need to pay for the use.”.

Sources indicate that “This principle has guided the entertainment industry for more than a century,” he continues. “Whether it can continue to protect Americans may be decided in the coming weeks. The No Fakes Act would create a federal prohibition on creating nonconsensual digital replicas of any person’s voice or likeness — famous or not.”.

In a recent development, the No Fakes Act, Lourd indicates, “would apply a tried-and-true formula to the A.I. era: control, consent and compensation. It would set a uniform federal standard to replace outdated, ill-fitting state laws, many of them written with an analog world in mind. Its supporters include all sides of the table: SAG-AFTRA, the union representing actors and other performers; the Motion Picture Association, representing the studios; and tech companies including IBM, Google and OpenAI.”.

Earlier this month, Lourd told Deadline’s Dominic Patten, that the challenges around AI are “about the fundamental relationship between technological progress and creative rights, and who determines the value of creative work, who decides how that work is used, and whether creators will share in the opportunities AI creates.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

According to recent reports, when you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a substantial "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be said for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

In a recent development, because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before new models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

Sources indicate that price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

In the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The issue isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

According to recent reports, the key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a newly introduced tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

It has been revealed that to avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

If you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

Split Radiance Cascades

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jacktollenaar

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Radiance cascades is a technique that massively improves global illumination without much extra cost or accumulation.
  • For this article I'll assume you already know the basics of RC, if not I really recommend the interactive tutorial from jason.today or the article from MAX Here is a quick recap as well.
  • Sources indicate that the main point of RC is combining the samples/rays for our GI in a way that utilizes them most effectively.This results in a more correct output with less samples.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Radiance cascades is a technique that massively improves global illumination without much extra cost or accumulation. In this article I'll go over the recent technique of Ray Splitting which allows the use of RC (Radiance cascades)in 3D without huge costs, and how to implement it. Note that the code examples are modified for clearability, so might not fully work.

For this article I'll assume you already know the basics of RC, if not I really recommend the interactive tutorial from jason.today or the article from MAX Here is a quick recap as well.

Sources indicate that the main point of RC is combining the samples/rays for our GI in a way that utilizes them most effectively.This results in a more correct output with less samples. The way of combining this relies on the penumbra hypothesis. Which states that, when you are close to a light source you need fewer rays (less angular resolution) to find the light.

In addition when you are close to a light you need more probes (spatial resolution) to get correct shadows.

To interpolate the half shadow, we need the light at both sides. Further away this spacing can be bigger to still get probes on both sides.

By merging layers ranging from (high resolution, low direction count) to (low resolution, high direction count) that correspond to an interval of the ray, we get best of both of these in the range that matters.

Sources indicate that RC requires storing our light into a grid of probes. This becomes a problem in 3D due to the massive memory cost that introduces. since probe counts scale ^3.

Even if we would only put this around the camera it would cost way too much memory to get a decent resolution.Luckily we only need probes where we need light, which is on all visible surfaces.So we need a way to only put probes on visible geometry.

To only spawn probes on visible surfaces, we reconstruct world positions from the screen.We round these positions to a grid of cells.

According to recent reports, to store our light in these cells we need a buffer of probes. To allocate this we use a hashtable. Creating a hash for each cell allows us to promptly allocate a slot for each of these without much fighting between threads.We also store an AppendBuffer with a list of the probes we allocated, this will be used later to launch our next passes indirectly.(this somewhat goes against the use of the hashtable, but the table will be needed more later)We clear and fill this table every frame and with this we get a table of sparsely allocated probes.

We can visualize/debug our probes in a separate pass.

With this gather pass we now have a single cascade of probes allocated.However we need multiple cascades of lowering resolution to do RC. For this we need to fill separate hashtables for each cascade, we could just re-run our shader for each cascade but that would be very innefficient. We already have our highest detail probes and there are significantly less of them than we have pixels. So instead of running over all pixels again, we can just go over all the probes we just allocated, for each of these we just halve their position to get the cascade above it. Any duplicates we get from this are handled by the hashtable.We run this bottom up for all cascades. The number of cascades we need is somewhat arbitrairy based on your scene size i'll be using 4.

Note that when visualizing your higher cascades you need to shift your positions when creating the key.

Normally to get the lighting at every probe, we shoot a set amount of rays into random directions from each probe.This however comes with quite a few complications.Ray counts become very massive with good enough spatial and angular resolution. But the main problem is probe positioning, since our probes are in a grid they are not aligned with the surfaces which can cause a bunch of rays to shoot below the surface. This can cause overocclusion and light leaking, and also makes it so we cannot shoot rays in just a hemisphere.

The 2 red rays in this probe here got unfairly blocked because the probe is too far into the ground.

This would cause dark splotches in our lighting.So instead we can trace the rays from reconstructed world positions and put these into the probes that are at that spot.This way rays are sent from real geometry avoiding this problem.

Here the blue rays are sent from the position gotten from the screen, then moved into the closest probe.

According to recent reports, however, in RC each cascade does not contain the full ray, only a interval/segment of it. Sending multiple rays for each interval at each pixel would be quite inefficient. Instead we do it the other way around, we trace the full ray and pick the interval (and thus cascade) that it would have hit in based on its hit distance. We fill the hit interval's cascade with the lighting, and then mark transparancy / that a ray traveled through them in the cascades below the hit one.

The red ray hit inside the second cascade, and thus is binned into the second and first cascade.

It has been revealed that we store this in multiple bins per probe, one for each direction. We need to lay out these directions evenly and most importantly in a way that scales so that our merging evenly combines them into lower cascades. For shooting each ray we can just pick a random direction in a hemisphere at our hit.

With this we should now have every cascade filled with its interval of light.If we display this by just averaging all bins in an output pass, we can see the rings of light this contains.

We now want to merge these intervals together so we can get our entire path of light. We do this by going through our cascades from top down. We need to interpolate the directions and probes. Starting with directions, since our directions are evenly mapped to 4 times more in the above cascade we evenly interpolate these in our own cascade.

Sources indicate that however we need to also keep in account the transparency in this merging. If a ray was already blocked in the direction we're merging in the lower cascade/interval we shouldn't merge it downwards.

Here the middle interval is blocked, so we should not merge the light from the last interval, or it will leak in front of the wall.

In a recent development, this merges our directions from the closest probe. Instead we want to check all the above probes and blend between them.For this we need to keep in mind probe spacing, each lower cascade has 8 probes inside 1 upper probe. So we shouldnt evenly blend.

According to recent reports, it's also key to keep in mind that our grid is sparse, meaning the 8 surrounding probes will probably not all be there. This can be resolved by only weighing and sampling the probes that actually exist. Additionally, not all our probes are of the same quality. The amount of rays a probe contains and thus how accurate it is, is based on its visibility on the screen. We should also adjust for this, giving a higher weight to probes that contain more rays.

With this we now have our full ray inside of the lowest cascade. To display this in our output shader, we have to merge the directions of the cascade into 1 value for each pixel, using the normal of the pixel to weigh the probes.

At the moment we have a even grid of probes, which works fine for small scenes. But our probes get very small on the screen further away.This has 2 major problems. We shoot our rays from the screen, so the number of rays in a probe is based on how many pixels it occupies on the screen. So very small probes only get one ray or maybe even less.Secondly, the number of probes we spawn explodes further away which costs a lot of memory and is expensive to merge.By adding a form of LODs to our probes we solve both these problems, at only the cost of lower resolution lighting far away.This is very similar to cascaded shadow maps which makes naming confusing and thus we call them LODs/Levels.For each higher LOD we also halve the resolution similarly to our higher cascades although we keep the direction count the same. To do this we just halve our cell position each level. However for this we need to add a level index to our per probe key. We need to do this since our halved positions can overlap with the lower level.We can just bitshift this index after the rest of our key.Since everything else uses the hashtable, this should automatically work with the rest of our code assuming we calculate the key in the same way.

In a recent development, this fixes a lot of flickering or overallocation further away, however it creates massive seams where the LODs change.So we want to blend in between these seams. To do this we keep some probes of overlap, allocating probes of both levels and also binning the ray into both.Wherever we calculate our level we instead calculate the range, making sure to keep correct weights so we do not double the light at the seam.

This should result in smooth, although flickering results.

Due to the benefits of splitting & merging with RC our single frame result is already pretty good. But since we still send random rays, there is still some flickering especially in probes that did not get many rays. We can fix this by accumulating our probes over time. This doesnt come with the drawbacks of most temporal effects. Since our probes are spatially stable, there is no smearing from bad reprojection. And since there is not a lot of noise in after a single frame there is barely any ghosting. So the only drawback is slower lighting updates.

Example of smearing using Lumen.

No smearing or much ghosting with RC.

Industry observers note that right now we clear and allocate the hashtable every frame, so our probe index moves every frame. To temporally accumulate we want our probes to keep the same index, so that we keep the old frame's result in their spot in the buffer. One way of doing this is by adding a layer of indirection to our hashtable, instead of storing the index into our data buffer in the table we store an index into another list of indices. That way we can add a pass that re-allocates our previous frame's results with the same index as the data. We also need to keep track of the lifetime of probes, to know which probes to reallocate or not, and resetting their lifetime if they are on screen.

In a recent development, the hashtable should now be stable, you can test this using the debug output code from earlier, outputting the index. Probes shouldn't change color unless they go off the screen. With stable probes temporally accumulating is easy, when going over the probes (in the merge pass or in a separate pass) we just re-add the probes accumulated light and weights with a falloff. With that you should now have clean single bounce GI.

According to recent reports, at the moment light only bounces once from where we are looking. Things only start looking really good when we do multiple bounces. To achieve this we need to trace 1 extra bounce ray everywhere, from which we can get infinite bounces over time. To get one bounce, we just shoot an extra light ray from the hits of our primary ray. To do this we output our hit positions and normals in our ray generation shader, then run a second one from that spot.

The first hit is stored, then another random ray is sent from that hit position.

In a recent development, this gives us a single real bounce, but increasing this to more would be very expensive. Instead we can sample the probes to apply GI to this, with the temporal accumulation that gives us an extra bounce every frame. However since our probes are only allocated where we are looking, we wouldn't be able to get this bounce light from outside of the screen, since there are no probes to sample from. To resolve this we allocate a separate secondary probe cache for this, we allocate extra probes at the hit positions of our primary ray. We fill these with radiance from the bounce ray, in the same way as our primary ray. To accumulate this to multiple bounces, we sample this cache at the hits of our primary and secondary rays.

In one frame we send the primary ray, which allocates a probe filled with the bounce ray. The next frame a different bounce ray hits the same secondary probe. Since it samples the cache it then also contains the previous bounce. Over frames this stacks to infinite bounces.

According to recent reports, this gives us infinite bounces, however it is limited to only the area covered by the single bounce ray, since that one allocates the secondary probes.We can re-use almost our whole system for this secondary probe. We already have LODs over distance, by allocating the secondary probes at at least 2 LODs higher it can fit into the same hashtable/probes without conflicts. If we also add these to the active probes the merge pass will merge their cascades as well. With that we get nice looking multi bounce GI.

It has been revealed that for simplicity I kept out a lot of optimizations or better ways to do things. I won't go over how to fully optimize but will briefly go over the main improvements that can be done to get this running well.

One substantial improvement in quality is choosing directions in a better way, at the moment we choose completely random directions.But there are multiple semi random sequences that accumulate to good results significantly quicker.By using a deposit count per probe as an index into something like the R2 sequence or blue noise, direction coverage accumulates significantly faster.

Apart from tracing, our merging & applying pass is the most expensive.It's sampling a lot of data across a low amount of threads.For example the bin merging can be done across threads, loading the 8 probes together and having each thread load a bin, merging them as a group.

Raytracing cost is by far the most expensive part.We can skip a percentage of pixels every frame to reduce cost significantly, although with the drawback of slower accumulation and thus more ghosting.Balancing this with probe sizes can improve the accumulation but at the cost of light resolution.This allows for a nice way of tweaking quality vs performance. It might also be worth replacing (some of) the rays with cheaper ones like screen space rays or sampling an sdf or voxel approximation of the world.

Almost all of the cost of this goes to actual tracing. For my implemention in Unreal on my 5070 Laptop GPU in San Miguel the cost of RC is about ~2ms depending on probe sizing.Although with ~13ms on top of raytracing at 2spp (1 primary 1 bounce) and another ~2ms for depositing the rays.The expensive tracing cost is very variable, depending on scene size and tracing performance in general.

The main points of error are light leaking in spots smaller than a (secondary) probe, and softer shadows. (presumably due to not enough base directions).

"Split Radiance Cascades: Real-Time Global Illumination via Sparse Radiance Probes": https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20384.

Jason Mcghee's article: https://jason.today/rc.

RC Wiki: https://radiance.wiki/.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest horror movies of the year, "Obsession," finally landed on Netflix this week, where Inde Navarrette's unhinged performance will no doubt haunt even more people's nightmares. If you’re still reeling from its tense atmosphere and wonder what other horror movies on Netflix capture that same sense of creeping dread and paranoia, I've got you covered.

It has been revealed that I watch a lot of horror movies, and my top three picks for what to watch after "Obsession" are sure to fit the vibe you're looking for. Two of them come from acclaimed horror series director Mike Flanagan, while the third is a slept-on horror mystery thriller with a perfect 100% score on Rotten Tomatoes that flips the haunted house trope on its head.

So without further ado, let's dive into the best horror movies on Netflix to watch after "Obsession.".

Just like "Obsession," "Hush" is another example of a simple premise executed well. It's also helmed by Mike Flanagan before he established himself as the king of TV horror with "The Haunting of Hill House," "Midnight Mass" and "Carrie." This slasher movie stars Flanagan's wife and long-time collaborator Kate Siegel as Maddie, a deaf and mute woman who becomes the target of a masked killer.

Industry observers note that it's lean, tightly wound horror movie that wrings a surprising amount of tension from its simple premise. The isolated setting of a house in the remote woods also adds to the atmosphere of constant unease, like you're being watched. And while Maddie is relentlessly stalked and tormented by the killer, she's never reduced to a helpless victim, which makes this one of the more empowering genre entries.

Sources indicate that with remarkable direction from Remi Weekes (who also wrote the screenplay), strong performances from the whole cast ("Doctor Who’s" Matt Smith has a small role) and plenty of terrifying moments, "His House" is a certified chiller — and one of the best Netflix horror movies. Whenever I recommend essential horror movies to get non-horror fans into the genre, "His House" tops the list.

In a recent development, "His House" follows a young refugee couple, Bol (Sope Dirisu) and Rial (Wunmi Mosaku), who are granted asylum in a small English town after fleeing war-torn South Sudan. They struggle to adjust, and straining their relationship further is the supernatural terror haunting their home that seems connected to their past. But while Rial insists something is not right and wants to move, Bol worries that making waves could get them deported. And so the two are left on their own to face whatever's haunting them.

Watch "His House" on Netflix now.

Industry observers note that another one from Flanagan (can you tell I'm a fan?), this trippy horror movie adds a fresh perspective to a familiar framework, where a cursed mirror not only warps the minds of the main characters, but leaves the audience questioning what's real and what's a hallucination. Noted mirror is responsible for the deaths of Kaylie (Karen Gillan) and Tim's (Brenton Thwaites) parents, who began acting strange and talking to the apparition of a dark-haired woman (Siegel) before they passed.

According to recent reports, adding to this disorientation, "Oculus" shift between two timelines: when the siblings were young and first witnessing the mirror's horrible influence, and then 11 years later when they come back to put an end to its demented reign of terror for good. Gillan gives a gloriously unhinged performance as her obsession (haha, get it?) with finally proving the mirror's curse is real ends up being her downfall when her carefully laid intends start falling apart.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • You can cancel your Prime subscription via web browser by first logging into your Amazon account.
  • Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.
  • Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can cancel your Prime subscription via web browser by first logging into your Amazon account. Amazon has a Cancel Your Prime Membership button on its support page to launch the process, or you can follow the steps detailed on Amazon's page:.

Head to Amazon.com in your web browser.

Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Note that Amazon requires a bunch of clicks to finalize your cancellation, giving you lots of “opportunities” to change your mind.

Open the Amazon Shopping app on your mobile device.

Click the three horizontal lines on the bottom right.

Under Shop by Category, select Prime.

On the top bar, slide all the way to the end and select Help.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

As mentioned, closing your account will immediately end your access. Amazon also offers you the option to pause your benefits and billing temporarily instead of canceling them completely. Either way, your Amazon account is still active—you simply won’t have Prime benefits.

Finally, if you have other subscriptions connected to your Prime account, those will end when your billing is up. And if you signed up for Prime through the Android mobile shopping app or the Prime Video Android app, you’ll have to go through Google Subscription to manage your membership.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

In a recent development, nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In a recent development, yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Watermelon Pictures and the Film Committee at Media City Qatar have revealed a planned strategic partnership to develop and co-produce a slate of films telling stories from the Global South.
  • The partnership marks a significant expansion into larger-scale, mainstream production for Watermelon Pictures.
  • Badie Ali and Hamza Ali released their Chicago-based production and distribution company in 2024, with a mission to amplify Palestinian and other under-represented voices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watermelon Pictures and the Film Committee at Media City Qatar have revealed a planned strategic partnership to develop and co-produce a slate of films telling stories from the Global South.

The partnership marks a significant expansion into larger-scale, mainstream production for Watermelon Pictures.

Badie Ali and Hamza Ali released their Chicago-based production and distribution company in 2024, with a mission to amplify Palestinian and other under-represented voices.

Until now, the firm has focused mainly on distribution, with recent releases including The Voice of Hind Rajab, El Sett, Who Killed Alex Odeh? and American Doctor. Related Stories News Egyptian Music Star Mohamed Mounir Gets Biopic - Doha Industry Days News 'Al Hayba' Star Taim Hasan To Play Syrian Whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan In Neon-Backed 'Caesar' Biopic.

Industry observers note that its cofounders recently signaled to Deadline that they were working on a development slate, without going into detail. Watch on Deadline.

The strategic partnership aims to combine Qatar’s infrastructure and resources as it seeks to grow the film and TV sector at home and regionally, and Watermelon’s access to leading talent, established distribution infrastructure, and understanding of what resonates with audiences.

“When we founded Watermelon Pictures, our vision was to bring powerful stories to the big screen with an unwavering commitment to authenticity,” remarked Watermelon Pictures cofounder Badie Ali.

“Our partnership with the Film Committee at Media City Qatar is a major step toward realizing that promise, allowing us to tell these stories on a larger scale while remaining true to the people and places at their heart.”.

Under the partnership, the parties would aim to shoot projects substantially in Qatar or structure them as Qatari co-productions.

They would also seek to involve Doha-based post-production companies and help eligible projects access the Qatar Screen Production Incentive (QSPI), creating opportunities for local crews, businesses, and creative talent while strengthening Qatar’s position as an international production hub.

Sources indicate that “Through this partnership, we want to give filmmakers the resources to tell stories rooted in their communities and bring them to audiences around the world. We also want the films we support to create work for crews and businesses in Qatar and give them experience they can carry into their next production,” remarked Hassan Al Thawadi, Chairman of the Film Committee at Media City Qatar.

It has been revealed that the Film Committee and Watermelon Pictures will jointly identify projects for the initial slate. The proposed partnership is subject to definitive agreements and the required approvals, with projects to be considered individually. More details on specific projects are soon to be announced.

Sources indicate that “Too many compelling stories and perspectives, including those of Arab and Muslim communities, have historically been underrepresented in mainstream cinema. We see an enormous opportunity to change that. Our planned slate will span genres, challenge perceptions, and, above all, entertain. Our ambition isn’t simply to create space in the industry. It’s to compete at its highest level,” mentioned Watermelon Pictures cofounder Hamza Ali.

The announcement of the planned partnership was made during the Film Committee’s Doha Industry Days, running from November 19 to 21 within the framework of the Doha Film Festival.

Industry News: Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions.
  • While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, remarked last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”.

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”.

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:.

In fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

Sources indicate that the law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that 2026 has been a pretty decent year for latest movies so far, but that doesn’t mean we’ve escaped the usual problem of some genuinely entertaining releases slipping under the radar. One such film is “They Will Kill You,” a gloriously bonkers mash-up of survival, comedy and horror that pits a tough-as-nails woman against a group of seriously unhinged cult members. The whole thing feels like a fever dream, with outrageous violence, ridiculous twists and enough carnage to keep you wondering what on earth you’re watching.

In a recent development, thankfully, Prime Video has now added “They Will Kill You” to its library, which I’m hoping will give this overlooked gem a chance to find a much bigger audience. Its theatrical run certainly didn’t do it any favors, with the movie reportedly earning approximately $19 million worldwide against a production budget of $20 million, making it a box office disappointment. That’s a shame, because while it’s not a perfect film by any means, it’s certainly not a bad one.

In a recent development, in fact, I’d argue it’s one of the more entertaining horror releases of the year so far. It knows exactly how ridiculous it wants to be and has plenty of fun with its increasingly chaotic set pieces. I left the theater genuinely shocked by some of the things I witnessed, but also grinning at just how much fun I'd had. If you missed it on the big screen, its arrival on Prime Video is a pretty good excuse to put that right, and here’s why.

“They Will Kill You” follows Asia Reaves (Zazie Beetz), a young woman who takes a live-in housekeeping job at The Virgil, a luxurious New York City apartment building, hoping to find her missing younger sister, Maria (Myha'la). However, Asia soon discovers that the building’s wealthy residents are hiding a terrifying secret: they’re members of a satanic cult that has been sacrificing unsuspecting workers for decades.

Industry observers note that when the residents attempt to make Asia their latest victim, they quickly discover she’s not quite as helpless as they expected. Trapped inside the building with seemingly no way out, Asia must fight her way through its corridors and take on an increasingly dangerous group of attackers. With time running out and Maria caught up in the cult’s plans, Asia faces a brutal fight to get them both out alive.

I’ll admit, I was a little worried “They Will Kill You” might struggle to stand out, especially arriving shortly after “Ready or Not 2,” which has a pretty similar premise involving two sisters trying to escape a cult. Thankfully, Zazie Beetz gives this film a flavor of its own. She’s an absolute badass, throwing herself into some wonderfully chaotic fight scenes and getting covered in blood more times than I can count. There’s also a noticeably angrier edge to this movie, which I really appreciated. It’s a welcome addition to the horror-comedy genre that isn’t afraid to get properly nasty.

Storytelling isn’t exactly the film’s strong suit, and I wouldn’t say it does anything particularly compelling with its characters or central plot. But that’s not really why I’d recommend it. The real draw is the action, inventive kill scenes and completely unhinged body horror. There are also some wonderfully ridiculous twists involving the cult that had me laughing, while the final act goes so completely off the rails that I was practically squealing (little hint there). It’s an absolute hoot, and I had a ridiculous amount of fun watching it.

In a recent development, I also really enjoyed the film’s visual style. Director Kirill Sokolov uses graphic compositions that sometimes resemble comic-book panels, alongside unusual framing and some wonderfully eccentric camera angles. There are moments when the whole thing almost feels like you’re watching a video game, particularly during its more elaborate fight sequences. Yes, it’s a little unconventional, but I thought it worked brilliantly with the film’s exaggerated violence and chaotic energy. It gives “They Will Kill You” a distinct visual identity that helps it stand apart from other horror-comedies.

There’s definitely a lack of genuine character connection here, largely because the story doesn’t give you much to work with, but Beetz is such a compelling screen presence that you naturally find yourself rooting for her anyway. She’s more than capable of carrying the film, and I’d happily watch her take on another ridiculous survival scenario. I also think “They Will Kill You” has some serious cult classic potential. It might not have found its audience at the box office back in March, but I wouldn't be surprised if it earns a lot more love in the years ahead as more people discover it. Sometimes all a film needs is a second chance, and this one certainly deserves it.

Stream "They Will Kill You" on Prime Video now.

According to recent reports, she heads to the cinema every week as a tradition, no matter what’s showing. For her, movies aren’t just entertainment — they’re a ritual, a comfort, and a constant source of inspiration. When she’s not at her desk or at the cinema, you’ll probably find her deep into a horror video game on her PC.

As a filmmaker who knows something about love with the Zendaya starring tennis love triangle pic, Challengers, and Oscar winning gay romance, Call Me By Your Name, we spoke with Guadagnino on the latest Crew Call as to what pulled him into the OpenAI-verse. Watch on Deadline.

Take a listen below. Essentially, it’s about about a bunch of young mad, narcissistic scientists acting like flawed Greek Gods in San Francisco:.

Well before its theatrical release, Artificial generated a lot of controversy as its original studio, Amazon MGM Studios, backed away from the movie out of fear of OpenAI. That’s because Amazon has a $50 billion investment in the Altman non-profit.

However, unlike the Facebook camp back when Social Network was getting released in 2010, there’s been zero ill will coming from Altman or OpenAI about Guadaganino’s film. In fact, you could say they’re great sports.

In a sit-down with the Vanity Fair podcast, Altman notes he “did not” coerce Amazon to drop Artificial. “I don’t know anyone else who did,” he added, “I didn’t speak to Jeff Bezos.”.

In fact, Guadagnino brazenly shot the pic outside Altman’s house in San Francisco. The filmmaker tells us about that. For Altman, he was giddy about running into his onscreen doppelgänger, Andrew Garfield: “One morning, I was walking down the street to get coffee and there were all these cameras and there was a guy dressed exactly like me with the same backpack, walking so much, I felt like I was in a weird glitch or a simulation.”.

Altman emphasized to Vanity Fair that Garfield “did walk like me.”.

In a recent development, while Altman hasn’t seen Artificial, his reaction to the trailer is, “I don’t think they’re going for accuracy, so in that sense it doesn’t bother me. They’re trying to make a good movie and maybe it will be good. It won’t be good as an accurate depiction, except for the walk. I’m sure they’ll get other parts right at least accidentally.”.

One of the jaw dropping moments shown in the Artificial trailer is Altman having a bunker in his wine country estate loaded with guns.

“That is an example of an inaccuracy,” Altman told Vanity Fair, “There’s no bunker with firearms on the wall.”.

“I have a survivalist mindset,” Altman admitted, “but I don’t have a setup that is depicted in that trailer.”.

Guadagnino tells Deadline, “I have validated the validating information that has been vetted: He does have guns.”.

Industry observers note that while the filmmaker experienced zero pushback from OpenAI and Altman during production on the Simon Rich script, he says “We were very careful that everything that was in the movie had to be approved legally, so that we were not bending facts and reality for our narrative purposes. But, because the truth in this case is more extraordinary than any fiction, that was okay. Because we had the drama, we had the juice.”.

When it came to Amazon exiting Artificial, Guadagnino had a Zen mindset: “I was cool because I like disruptions, very much.”.

“Their decision to give the movie to us to find another home was truly honorable, because they could have written off the movie and (remarked) ‘Bye-bye’.”.

As far as Artificial being a hot potato that no studio wanted to handle, except NEON, Guadagnino asserts that “All the speculation about nobody wanting the movie; I like to think that there was the need (by the media) to fill blank pages with nothing.”.

It has been revealed that for off the bat, per Guadagnino, NEON was first, front and center in their passion to takeover the project after CAA screened it for them. Listen above for more details.

When it comes to the paranoia out there that AI is the catalyst for human extinction in ten years, the filmmaker tells Deadline, “I don’t have trust and I don’t have faith in humans.”.

Industry observers note that his suspicions about AI stem from growing up during the Cold War. “I remember very well in 1985 when Chernobyl happened,” he adds.

And there’s myriad reasons for concerns about AI, from a Chatbot being at the center of 16-year old Adam Raine’s suicide, to AI trespassing and impostering another manufacturer’s security space.

We also talk with the Call Me By Your Name Best Picture Oscar nominee on why Andrew Garfield was the right guy to play Altman, and the Open AI Boss’ sincerity when it comes to creating guardrails for the technology.

Breaking: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2358 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Linebender

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago.
  • The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong.
  • Sources indicate that adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits announced since that blog post (see 2026 survey), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI.

The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative.

Sources indicate that adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia.

The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance?

For these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things.

My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the crucial quality criteria.

I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted. Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI. However, SwiftUI has performance challenges (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front.

While desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different. Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are vital for an app to look and feel native. One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right. In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems.

Thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust. I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native. I believe 1Password has this architecture. This is also the "Phoenix" proposal for Discord on mobile, while using GPUI on desktop.

Recent findings suggest that that said, there's been considerable progress in trying to build mobile UI entirely in Rust. Below is a short screencast of the editor demo in android-view. You can see that a lot of IME functionality works, including swiping, moving the cursor by rolling the space bar, and deleting in semantic chunks. Not shown in the video below, but composition regions (needed for CJK) also work, and there's basic accessibility through AccessKit.

One of the substantial unsolved problems as of the 2022 blog post was text layout. It is of course a hard problem to get right. I’m pleased to say that the ecosystem now has a good solution, in the form of Parley. It’s gotten there as a result of sustained investment from Google, Canva, and Dioxus (now Cognition), as well as contributions from the community. It seems to be used in the majority of newly introduced Rust UI toolkits. In addition, to help mitigate the risk of monoculture, Cosmic Text is a viable alternative.

AccessKit was just getting started in 2022, but is now solid infrastructure as well, and used by most UI toolkits. I should note, though, there is a difference between a good integration and a box ticking exercise. And there is more work to be done, for example to make rich text editing fully accessible. One other problem I'd like to see addressed is performance degradation when accessibility is enabled. This is a problem for egui in particular, as it has to build and diff a tree each animation frame, undercutting the benefits of its underlying immediate mode design.

Industry observers note that one topic I talked about extensively in the 2022 blog post is leveraging the system compositor. This matter is even more pressing today, especially with the increased importance of video. You really want a video playing in a hardware accelerated layer when possible, and on low end devices it’s the only hope for getting smooth frame rates.

Industry observers note that there has been some progress, notably the subduction library, but it certainly isn’t commonly integrated into UI toolkits yet. To do it well is a challenging problem, as the capabilities provided by the platform vary widely. Ideally there’s a rich and high level interface, something like CALayer on Apple platforms, and polyfills to implement that interface as well as possible on other platforms. On Android, when the task is something simple, like overlaying some GUI controls on a video, it would use SurfaceFlinger layers, but when it involves more sophisticated compositing, it would run shaders on the GPU.

This is absolutely something we should build, ideally as a high quality community project rather than something with dozens of vibe-coded forks. But even in the latter case it’s better for it to exist than not.

According to recent reports, one of the challenges of the Rust UI ecosystem is that different applications have different needs. The idea of a single, unified UI for completely general purpose use may be behind us, especially now that LLMs can optimize and fine tune for specific use cases.

That’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode. Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler. And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well. However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well. In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder. To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and update the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev). And of course, it pulls strongly towards a model of re-rendering everything every frame rather than exploiting layers in the compositor.

In a recent development, for this reason among others, I am not impressed by the choice of the ArtCraft projects to use egui. I do think egui is a really good implementation of the immediate mode paradigm in Rust, and it does solve a number of problems (including accessibility, something mainline Iced does not yet support), but it wouldn’t be my first choice for productivity and design applications. The egui README is quite honest on the advantages and disadvantages, and is worth consulting.

One theme that’s emerging from trying to do LLM-assisted software engineering well is having clearly scoped modules, ideally with solid specifications of what the module does. Within a module, given clear objectives such as performance and robustness against adverse inputs, an LLM can do very well.

This philosophy is in tension with what has historically worked well. People reasonably choose a UI toolkit based on how good it looks. In particular, Apple UI frameworks have an immense amount of design knowledge baked in, especially in the defaults. With very little effort, it’s possible for a developer to make an app that looks and feels like a Mac app, even if not very polished.

I think in the future we should be moving toward a separation of design and execution. Both are hard problems, but very different. I’m especially excited about how much room there is to improve the execution side when really optimizing. As discussed in the 2022 blog post, the computer science core of a UI toolkit is an incremental computation engine.

Industry observers note that having a good spec at the interface between design and execution is critically crucial. As a general strategy, I suggest adapting web standards, but not following them slavishly. Web standards are an impressive and important artifact. A huge amount of time and energy has gone into producing them, and there’s also a lot of care to making things work cross-platform. The extensive WPT tests are the true magic of the spec, aiding correctness in the multiple high quality open source implementations. All this goes a long way to explaining why Electron is popular.

Recent findings suggest that that mentioned, strictly adhering to web standards has serious downsides. DOM is slow and memory-intensive; a lighter weight tree representation with a bulk mutation interface might serve the need of GUI apps better. Full CSS style resolution and layout is also expensive, though CSS is a rich and powerful way to describe styling. A subset of CSS carefully curated for efficiency might be useful. I’ve done experiments in implementing selectors as an efficient state machine that supports incremental evaluation, at the expense of fancier CSS features such as sibling selectors.

Sources indicate that the Web is also lacking a solid way to represent virtualized lists, a core feature of every efficient UI toolkit. A spec here requires nailing down the interface with the data model, preserving incrementality.

In a recent development, blitz, as a modular browser engine, is well placed to serve as the cornerstone of hybrid approaches borrowing heavily from Web specs, but also adapting them to be higher performance and more tightly integrated with platform capabilities. As just one example, it’s possible to start with Stylo as the CSS selector engine, and then replace it with a leaner, more efficient CSS engine if that proves to be practical.

One good example of separation of concerns into smaller modules is the Xilem/Masonry split. The Xilem reactive layer was designed to be independent of the actual elements it controls, and indeed it has instantiations both for DOM (which, among other things, is the infrastructure for the squircle interactive demo) and Masonry widgets. Masonry, on the other hand, was designed to be independent of the reactive layer and indeed the language for the layer above it.

By contrast, SwiftUI mashes together the low level widget implementation, the reactivity framework, and the language as well; Swift runtime reflection is part of the execution engine. Obviously SwiftUI has had a lot farther reach than Xilem, but my argument today is that we should reconsider assumptions as things are rapidly changing.

Sources indicate that given a UI design encoded in a certain way – which can be code, data, or a combination of the two in a DSL – an engine has a number of opportunities to optimize the execution of that design. Perhaps a lot of this section is gilding the lily, as a straightforward evaluation of the design in optimized Rust code will outperform almost any shipping GUI. But I’m interested in the limits of what performance is possible. Can we get silky smooth UI even on low end Android phones? I think the answer is yes, and the question worth exploring.

According to recent reports, one useful tactic may be separating out the static from the dynamic parts of the design, and precomputing the static parts. That in no way precludes the design having dynamic parts; it's just that it may be possible to avoid the cost of a fully dynamic implementation.

Another fruitful avenue for optimization is optimizing the use of layers, to be composited either using the system compositor or a lightweight GPU-accelerated polyfill. Using layers effectively can dramatically improve performance, mostly by avoiding re-rendering of parts of the interface that haven't changed. However, layers have a RAM cost, and using too many layers can actually slow things down, as allocating new layers has to go through calls to the underlying system. Getting this right is a tricky optimization problem, and a good use of either measurement or analysis. UI toolkits generally either use heuristics, which are not always perfect, or explicit hints (like .drawingGroup() in SwiftUI or RepaintBoundary in Flutter).

Industry observers note that for a deeper dive into performance questions, see A Critique of GPUI. Ideally, there aren't huge performance differences between UI toolkits, as all low hanging fruit should be picked. We expect implementations of system languages to be quite comparable in performance, but still tolerate wide discrepancies in GUI performance.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re scheduled for an upcoming hip or knee replacement surgery, you’re far from alone.
  • Prehab—a structured strengthening program you do before surgery—can help strengthen your knee and hip joints.
  • “Surgery addresses the damaged joint, but patients still need strength to regain mobility and participate in rehabilitation afterward,” says Kaylee LeCavalier, PT, DPT, SCS, CSCS, CAPS, a physical therapist and board-certified sports specialist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re scheduled for an upcoming hip or knee replacement surgery, you’re far from alone. The American Joint Replacement Registry, managed by the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, has surpassed 4.3 million hip and knee replacement procedures in its database. People heading into these operations have often spent months or years modifying how they move because of hip or knee pain, which can leave the muscles around the joints weaker than they should be.

The good news? Prehab—a structured strengthening program you do before surgery—can help strengthen your knee and hip joints. A 2026 systematic review found early benefits for pain management, mobility, and functionality in people who underwent knee replacement surgery.

“Surgery addresses the damaged joint, but patients still need strength to regain mobility and participate in rehabilitation afterward,” says Kaylee LeCavalier, PT, DPT, SCS, CSCS, CAPS, a physical therapist and board-certified sports specialist.

Here’s how early to start prehab, how often to do it, and the four moves that LeCavalier recommends before surgery.

In a recent development, “Building strength takes time, and starting earlier provides more opportunity to progressively increase resistance and improve physical capacity before surgery,” explains LeCavalier. “Research suggests benefits in programs lasting 6 to 8 weeks, but no optimal duration has been established.”.

In a recent development, if your surgery is closer than that, don’t dismiss the benefits of doing prehab. “Even with only a few weeks available, patients can still make meaningful progress toward preparing their bodies for surgery and recovery,” LeCavalier states.

It has been revealed that for most people, LeCavalier recommends doing strength training two to three days per week, and allowing for proper recovery between more intense sessions. However, how often you should train depends on your beginning strength, activity level, pain, and how well you tolerate the exercises.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Recent findings suggest that leCavalier recommends starting each session with a short warm-up, such as a few minutes of walking or stationary cycling, then move into the strengthening work with enough rest between sets to ensure you’re using proper technique. She stresses that “exercises need to provide enough resistance to challenge the muscles.”.

According to recent reports, bodyweight exercises are an excellent starting point if you have significant pain or limited strength in your knees or hips. As the moves get easier, you can add weights, use stronger resistance bands or progress to harder variations. A good sign that you’re ready to progress is when you can consistently complete the sets and reps with proper form and control and without a significant increase in pain or swelling during exercise or the following day.

The leg press helps strengthen the major muscles around your hips and knees and is one of the few exercises with research behind it before knee replacement.

In a recent development, both of these moves help build the strength you need to get up from a seated position and support your body weight during daily activities. Sit-to-stands are often a more beginner-friendly exercise, while squats are a foundational compound exercise that you can progress toward.

Your hip abductors help stabilize your pelvis when you stand on one leg, which is essential for walking and climbing stairs.

Step-ups focus on one leg at a time, which can help improve mobility and strength in your hips and knees.

According to recent reports, one of the best headphone deals right now is for my favorite headphones: Sony's 1000X series has been around since 2016, with each fresh model improving on the previous iteration; the latest being the Sony WH-1000XM6, released in 2025. These are the best over-ear headphones I tested in 2025 (or ever, really). Right now, you can get the WH-1000XM6 headphones for $348 (originally $459.99), their lowest price ever during the early Black Friday sale from Amazon.

The XM6 headphones improve on what were already excellent headphones. Sony upped the count of microphones from eight to 12 when compared to the XM5, which improves more than just how well you sound to someone on a phone call. The microphones are used in almost all of its features, like ANC, Adaptive Sound Control, and the headphones' Ambient Sound mode. They hear your surroundings to adapt their features accordingly. If you switch from a noisy room to a quiet one, the XM6 can switch from ANC to "aware mode" (if you have Adaptive Sound Control on).

These headphones have a lot more features that you can nerd out on in their companion app. The audio quality is second to none, with the fully customizable EQ giving you plenty of options to get the sound how you like it. I really like being able to see what codec you're listening to in the app's main menu. That way, there's no guessing if you're getting the best audio quality or not. They will give you 30 hours of battery life with ANC on and 40 hours of juice with ANC off. There's an AUX (3.5mm) jack for wired listening, which is a nice touch for audiophiles who still rock iPod Classics (or is that just me?).

The XM6s were not just the best headphones of 2025, but are still the best ones of 2026 and likely to be the best ones for years to come. For $348, you'll be securing the best for a record-low price.

#108407. Reversing the Next-Page Prefetcher in Skylake-X
