Industry observers note that amazon's Black Friday 2026 sale has brought the Sonos Arc Ultra down to $849 from its usual $1,099, a $250 discount that marks its lowest price yet. PCMag named it the best soundbar of 2024 and gave it an “outstanding” rating in its review. Still, $849 is a lot to spend on a single soundbar, and anyone shopping on a tighter budget will find more affordable picks in our Fire TV soundbar roundup. For more editor-vetted tech deals, check out our comprehensive Black Friday coverage.

For those who can make room in their budget, the next thing to strategy around is space, since the Arc Ultra measures a little over 46 inches across and weighs about 13 pounds, making it a natural match for a larger TV. Despite all that width, it keeps a low profile at just under three inches tall, so it can sit beneath most screens without blocking the picture, or you can wall-mount it if you would rather keep your TV stand clear. All that size makes room for a 9.1.4-channel layout (a substantial step up from the original Arc) that gives Dolby Atmos effects more space to spread around and above you. Sonos also added a newly introduced Sound Motion driver that it says doubles the original Arc's bass, giving action scenes real weight without a separate subwoofer, though you can still add a Sub 4 later for more rumble.

In a recent development, at the other end of the sound spectrum, voices and dialogue come through clearly even at low volumes, and a Speech Enhancement mode lifts them further. Trueplay tuning then adjusts the sound to your room, with a quick version on Android and iOS and a more detailed one for iPhone owners. The biggest drawback is connectivity, since the Arc Ultra has a single HDMI eARC port with no passthrough, which can leave you short on inputs for a console or streaming box, and no optical port. It also lacks DTS:X support, a letdown for some Blu-ray collectors, and voice control is limited to Alexa or Sonos' own assistant, though Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and AirPlay 2 make streaming music from your phone easy.

If you want to experiment with a different approach, you might need to repeat much of that setup. And when you’re finished, you either keep paying for the machine or throw away the environment you’ve just prepared.

Developers have already been dealing with this for years, autonomous agents just make the problem more glaring.

It has been revealed that an agent might need a computer for five minutes to run tests, several hours to work on a codebase, or days to complete a larger task. It needs a filesystem, processes, networking, and the freedom to install and run software. It also needs somewhere to do all of this without unrestricted access to your laptop or production infrastructure.

We think the right abstraction is surprisingly simple: a real computer that you can create, use, fork, and discard as easily as any other cloud resource.

That’s the idea behind Avrea Sandboxes.

In a recent development, A lot of sandbox infrastructure is designed around executing a command or running a short-lived task. That’s useful, but sometimes you need more than an execution API, you’d actually want an entire machine.

One where you can install arbitrary software, run development servers, maintain files across sessions, and use a normal operating system. One that works equally well when controlled by a human over RDP or SSH or by an autonomous agent.

Avrea Sandboxes are full virtual machines, with hardware virtualization providing the isolation boundary.

We’ve made a few deliberate choices about the underlying infrastructure.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t a newly introduced idea. AWS Nitro is a good example of an architecture built around hardware-assisted virtualization and strong isolation. We think those properties should be the baseline for a cloud computer, not something users have to think about.

Second, we use the highest-performance hardware available: Apple M5 Max for Linux arm64, and highest base clock AMD Zen 5 EPYCs for Linux amd64 and Windows.

These are the same hardware platforms we’ve been optimizing for our CI infrastructure.

In a recent development, the performance is measurable. In RunsOn’s independent ARM runner benchmarks, Avrea’s M5 Max machines finished first among the tested configurations at 2, 4, and 8 vCPUs. On x86, Avrea also led the 4-vCPU combined build benchmark, completing the tested workloads in 6m58s compared with 18m18s on GitHub-hosted runners.

Different workloads will see different results, but the underlying point is that we’re not building sandboxes on a separate, lower-performance compute tier.

We’re taking the infrastructure we’ve already optimized for running demanding CI workloads and making it available as general-purpose computers.

There’s a tendency to measure how quickly a VM can start. That’s useful, but it’s only part of the story.

In a recent development, imagine creating a fresh machine to work on a repository. The VM might boot rapidly, but then you need to fetch Git objects, download dependencies, install tools, and build the project.

According to recent reports, for a short-lived environment, those steps can take longer than the actual task. This is particularly relevant for agents. If an agent creates a fresh environment for every task, or several environments to explore different approaches, repeatedly downloading the same dependencies becomes a substantial waste of time.

We’ve already spent a lot of effort solving this problem for CI, and Avrea Sandboxes benefit from the same acceleration infrastructure.

Sources indicate that for Git, we maintain datacenter-local mirrors to reduce the cost of fetching repositories. Sandboxes can initialize a repository during creation, so the code is already there when you connect, provided the preload succeeds.

For dependencies, we provide colocated package caches for npm, pnpm, pip, Cargo, Go, Maven, Gradle, and many other ecosystems. Repeated downloads can be served locally rather than fetched from upstream registries.

And for build outputs, repository-connected sandboxes can inherit the same configured caches used by CI workloads.

We’ve written about these mechanisms in more detail in our guide to GitHub Actions caching.

The impact can be substantial. In our Next.js benchmark, faster hardware reduced a cold build from 3m23s to 1m23s. With a warm Turborepo cache, the measured build step took just 1.4 seconds.

These figures compare specific CI build configurations and cache states; individual workload results vary. The same acceleration mechanisms are available to sandbox workloads.

Industry observers note that fast infrastructure isn’t just about fast CPUs. It’s about eliminating unnecessary work.

We care about time to useful work, not just time to boot.

Industry observers note that we branch source code all the time. We create a new branch to experiment, try an alternative implementation, or preserve something before making a risky change.

Why shouldn’t we be able to do something similar with an entire computer?

Recent findings suggest that suppose you’ve spent half an hour reproducing a difficult bug. You’ve installed the right dependencies, configured the environment, and finally reached the failing state. Now you want to try two different fixes.

Normally, you’d either modify the environment in place or recreate it somewhere else. Neither is particularly appealing.

With Avrea Sandboxes, you can pause and fork an eligible VM, creating an independent copy of its disk and machine configuration.

According to recent reports, you can then experiment with the copy while leaving the original untouched. The same approach works for automated workflows. Prepare an environment once, then fork it for separate experiments or parallel tasks. A human can inspect one copy while an agent works on another.

Forking is to computers what branching is to source code.

Sources indicate that there are differences, of course. A VM contains more than source files. It can contain credentials, installed software, configuration, and other sensitive state. Forking copies disk contents, not external side effects or running process memory. You still need to manage credentials and access appropriately.

At the moment, forking requires a supported paused sandbox; Linux amd64 is the platform with pause/resume support. Avrea’s dedicated ephemeral agent-sandbox service has a different lifecycle and doesn’t currently support forking.

Industry observers note that but the broader idea is interesting: a computer no longer has to be a unique environment that you carefully maintain or rebuild from scratch. It can be something you copy as part of normal work.

Industry observers note that the traditional cloud VM model is oriented around servers. You provision a machine, configure it, and keep it running until you no longer need it.

Industry observers note that but a development environment isn’t necessarily a server. You might need a computer for ten minutes to compile something, an hour to investigate a bug, or an afternoon to try a newly introduced framework.

Avrea Sandboxes are billed by the second, so you don’t need to commit to a long-running machine just to perform a short task. Networking is included in the price, without separate bandwidth metering.

And for supported Linux amd64 sandboxes, you can pause and resume the environment instead of starting from scratch. A normal pause preserves the disk; an optional memory-preserving pause can also retain running process state.

Sandboxes have configurable time limits and retention rules, so they aren’t intended to become permanent, forgotten servers.

Create a computer when you need it. Fork it when you want to experiment. Pause it when you want to come back. Delete it when you’re done.

A computer is much more useful when it can participate in the network normally.

According to recent reports, you might want to run a development server, expose a webhook endpoint, test an API, or share a preview with someone. These are common requirements for developers, but they’re equally relevant to agents that need to interact with external services or host temporary applications.

Avrea Sandboxes support public HTTPS endpoints for services running inside the VM.

According to recent reports, you can publish a port and receive an HTTPS URL with Avrea-managed TLS termination. The implementation supports HTTP/2, WebSockets, and streaming responses, with normal service limits.

No separate reverse proxy or certificate management is required. Published URLs are publicly reachable, so applications containing sensitive data should still implement authentication.

It has been revealed that the goal isn’t to replace every networking primitive with a proprietary abstraction. It’s to make ordinary networking convenient enough that you don’t have to think about infrastructure for a temporary development environment.

Here’s what a typical workflow looks like with the Avrea CLI.

You can also publish an application port during creation using --https-port 3000, making a development server accessible over HTTPS.

On a supported Linux amd64 sandbox, you can preserve the environment and fork it:.

Industry observers note that the commands are intentionally ordinary. Behind them is a complete virtual machine, predictable compute capacity, accelerated repository access, nearby caches, and a managed lifecycle.

The interesting part isn’t any individual command. It’s that you can create and manipulate whole computers without having to assemble an infrastructure stack around them.

AI agents are an obvious use case for this kind of infrastructure.

Sources indicate that an agent that can write code but has nowhere to execute it isn’t particularly useful. And giving autonomous software unrestricted access to a user’s machine is rarely a good default.

A separate VM gives the agent its own filesystem, processes, tools, and operating system, with a clear isolation boundary.

But we don’t think the underlying infrastructure should be designed exclusively for agents.

It has been revealed that A developer debugging a failing test and an agent attempting to fix it need essentially the same computing resources. The developer might interact through SSH, a terminal, or a remote desktop. The agent might interact through an API or command execution interface.

The computer itself doesn’t need to care who’s operating it.

We’ve also introduced dedicated agent sandboxes for coding-agent sessions. These are intentionally ephemeral and have different lifecycle rules from user-created sandboxes, but they build on the same general idea: give autonomous software an isolated place to work.

Need a clean environment to reproduce a bug? Create one. Want to test a risky dependency upgrade? Fork one. Need an agent to investigate something without touching your local machine? Give it a separate environment. Finished with the task? Delete it.

Cloud infrastructure has made compute programmable, but it hasn’t always made computers convenient.

Making that practical requires more than fast VM startup. It requires predictable hardware, efficient repository access, colocated caches, ordinary networking, and lifecycle operations that make environments easy to preserve or copy.

Industry observers note that we’ve already built much of that infrastructure for the fastest CI service. Avrea Sandboxes just make it available for more general use.

For developers, they’re powerful temporary workspaces. For agents, they’re isolated execution environments. For both, they’re simply computers that can be created when needed and discarded when they’re no longer useful.

Computers should be easy to create. They should be ready for work. And they should be forkable.

Get started with Avrea Sandboxes.

Upgrade, November 19, 4:46 p.m. ET: The release candidates are now available to public beta testers, with the same build numbers as the developer RCs.

It has been revealed that in addition to macOS 27.3 beta 2, Apple is also rolling out the first Release Candidates for macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.4. Here are the details.

Two weeks ago, Apple released macOS Tahoe 26.7.3 and Sequoia 15.8.3, along with macOS 27.2.1 Golden Gate, all of which included security fixes related to AirPlay, Bluetooth, and Messages, among others.

Today, the company released the first RCs for macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.4, along with the second developer beta for macOS 27.3.

As is usually the case with direct-to-RC rollouts, Apple’s notes mention only that the updates provide ”security fixes for your Mac.” The actual release notes will likely become available soon after Apple officially releases macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.4 in the coming weeks.

The build for macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 RC 1 is 24H319, and the build for macOS Tahoe 26.7.4 RC 1 is 25G422.

While many Yellowjackets fans are struggling to cope with the inevitable end, for its series creators, it was the right time to land the plane.

Discussing the fourth and final season with Deadline, Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson explained that they didn’t want to “run the risk of overstaying our welcome” with another season when they were reaching the conclusion “more rapidly.”.

It has been revealed that “We’d always remarked that we had pitched a five-season strategy, but we’d always given the caveat that we felt like the show would tell us when it wanted to end, and just in the breaking of this story, it started to feel like we were sort of moving towards the end more rapidly,” explained Nickerson. “And so, then the decision kind of became, ‘OK, do we sort of squeeze a lot into Season 4 or run the risk of overstaying our welcome out of the fifth season?’ We chose to try to squeeze it in, and that ended up really just kind of working out nicely from our perspective.

“The show has always had to be very kind of efficient, with the storytelling. It’s a double ensemble with a lot of story that we’re telling, and so I think we’ve gotten pretty good or comfortable kind of operating a at a certain pace and a certain kind of grammar, for lack of a better word, and so that was what we did,” he added. Watch on Deadline.

As Nickerson explained it was an “incredible gift” to know they were ending after Season 4, Lyle noted that they were “reinvigorated” to get to return to civilization, which had always been their proposal for the final season.

“We had been looking forward to that for so long now. It was part of the original pitch, and to finally get there—everything, when you’re pitching a show, it all feels like a pipe dream,” stated Lyle. “You don’t think you’re actually going to be able to do any of this, especially something that you know is only gonna be if you get a first season, a second season, a third season. So, to actually reach that point and get to dive in, it reinvigorated everybody.”.

Sources indicate that in Yellowjackets, a 1996 Fresh Jersey soccer team’s plane crashes in the Canadian wilderness, where they struggle to survive while they’re stranded for 19 months as a dark supernatural force seemingly lurks in the woods. Meanwhile, their adult counterparts cope with the memories of what went down in the wilderness.

With newly introduced episodes available to stream Fridays on Paramount+ with Premium Blueprint, the fourth and final season sees the Yellowjackets rescued and returned home, where they must adjust to civilization and take their secrets to the grave.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ChatGPT might be the first name that comes to mind when you think of AI, but Anthropic’s Claude has been building a compelling collection of features that could convince even longtime ChatGPT users to switch.

Sources indicate that with Anthropic now a publicly traded tech giant, more people are likely to discover Claude for themselves. And while both chatbots can help you write emails, analyze documents and tackle everyday tasks, Claude has some clever tricks that set it apart.

I've spent considerable time using both AI assistants, and what makes Claude particularly interesting right now is how it fits into the tools and routines you already use.

Here are five things worth trying.

One of the most underrated reasons to download Claude on your iPhone is how well it works with Apple's native apps.

Through its iOS integrations, Claude can add items to your existing Apple Reminders lists, draft calendar events and prepare text messages and emails.

According to recent reports, imagine planning Thanksgiving dinner with Claude. Once you've settled on a menu, you can ask the chatbot to add the ingredients to your grocery list in Reminders. There's no need to copy and paste everything into another app.

Although ChatGPT has its own scheduled reminders and integrates with Apple Intelligence, Claude offers more direct access to Apple Reminders through its mobile app.

Give it a try with a prompt like: "Plan five easy weeknight dinners for my family and add the ingredients to my grocery list in Apple Reminders.".

If you've been using ChatGPT for years, switching to another AI assistant can feel like starting a upcoming job where nobody knows you.

It has been revealed that anthropic has a clever solution. Claude offers a dedicated memory import feature that helps you transfer personal preferences, professional details and other information from competing chatbots.

Claude provides a prompt that you can paste into your existing AI assistant. Once it generates a summary of what it knows about you, simply copy the response into Claude's memory settings.

Recent findings suggest that you won't transfer your entire conversation history, but you can give Claude a substantial head start. And you don't need a paid subscription to try it.

Both ChatGPT and Claude now offer Skills, which are essentially reusable sets of instructions that teach AI how to perform specific tasks.

However, Claude has an advantage when it comes to bringing those instructions into the applications you already use for work.

The custom Skills you enable in Claude are also available through its Microsoft 365 add-ins for Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook.

Sources indicate that you could teach Claude how you like your business proposals formatted, how you organize monthly expenses or how you respond to customer emails. And rather than explaining your preferences every time you open a upcoming document, Claude can follow the instructions you've already established.

ChatGPT also supports Skills in some Office experiences, but Claude's integration spans all four applications.

Perhaps the most fascinating development in AI right now is that you don't necessarily need to write a prompt to teach a chatbot something new.

With Claude's workflow recording feature, Mac customers can demonstrate a task while Claude captures their screen, mouse clicks, keyboard activity and optional voice narration.

Claude then turns the demonstration into a reusable Skill that you can review and save.

In a recent development, think about all those little tasks you do on your computer every week. Maybe you organize receipts, patch a spreadsheet or compile information from several websites.

Instead of writing detailed instructions for an AI assistant, you can show Claude how you normally do the work.

OpenAI offers similar functionality through Codex's Record & Replay feature, but Claude makes this approach available through its general-purpose desktop assistant.

ChatGPT is excellent at generating images, but Claude takes a different approach to creative work.

Through its design tools, you can give Claude your existing logos, fonts, color palettes and design guidelines to establish a reusable visual identity.

You don't need to be a professional designer to appreciate the possibilities.

If you're starting a small business, running an Etsy shop or launching a newsletter, Claude can help establish a consistent look across your marketing materials, presentations and websites.

Rather than uploading the same reference images and explaining your preferred aesthetic every time, you can work from an established design system that Claude applies across projects.

ChatGPT can follow brand guidelines and reference templates, but Claude's dedicated design system offers a more structured approach to maintaining visual consistency.

I'm not giving up ChatGPT anytime soon, particularly when it comes to image generation and voice conversations. But Claude has become much more than an alternative chatbot for writing and coding.

Anthropic's approach to AI is particularly appealing if you want an assistant that adapts to the way you already work, rather than having to change your habits to accommodate your AI.

In a recent development, if you've never tried Claude, start with the free version. You might be surprised by how much it can do.

In a recent development, find the network fault in seconds, not hours. Upload a .pcap / .pcapng capture (gzip too) and PcapAnalyzer tells you what is failing, why, and what to check next. It runs on your own machine, so captures never leave your network.

Free and open source (Apache 2.0). Status: beta.

You need Docker with Docker Compose. On Windows, run the script from Git Bash or WSL.

Industry observers note that the script creates a random access token (shown once, stored in .env) and starts the app. When the build finishes, open http://localhost:8080, paste the token into the "API token" field (top right) and upload a capture, or click "Try the sample capture".

The app listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Do not expose it on a network without an authenticated reverse proxy: the API can use your AI account. QUICKSTART.md has the details, the AI setup and troubleshooting.

You need Python 3.9+, Node 20+ and tshark (installed with Wireshark).

In a recent development, open http://localhost:5173 and paste the same token. If tshark is not on your PATH, set TSHARK_PATH to the binary.

Industry observers note that pcapAnalyzer is a beta. It has been tested with synthetic fixtures and public sample captures, and the most useful feedback is a capture where it misses a problem or reports one that is not real. Please open an issue at https://github.com/sebaandrada-cell/PcapAnalyzer/issues and describe the case. Do not attach captures that contain real credentials or customer data; anonymise them first or describe the pattern.

The technical reference (JSON schema, detector thresholds, limits, API errors) is in README.es.md, in Spanish.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of consumers. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that fresh job listings on Apple’s website indicate the firm’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the company has also introduced fresh restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Last month, Apple declared plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access, with changes introduced in the macOS 27.3 beta that give users more granular control over which apps and information third-party AI agents can access.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted newly introduced job listings that offer a closer look at its intends to develop autonomous AI agents:.

According to recent reports, in one, Apple noted it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:.

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”.

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “blueprint and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Sources indicate that today’s report on the fresh job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring customers to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the organization could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the latest job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its aims for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how quickly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally launched its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, in this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity.
  • Recent findings suggest that to buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first announced. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

According to recent reports, in this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

Recent findings suggest that to buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

The simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you said) to your “Notes to self” note.

To take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.).

According to recent reports, all the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

According to recent reports, it’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.).

Industry observers note that there’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can strategy them better next time.

Industry observers note that you’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

In a recent development, but this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.).

The Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I mentioned it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

I never struggled to make out dialogue, even in action-heavy scenes, which is something the TV Soundbar’s big brother, the TV Soundbar Plus, struggled with.

So, might the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar be the budget model for you? To find out, keep reading this Amazon Fire TV Soundbar review.

24 inches x 2.5 inches x 3.5 inches.

The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar has a lot going for it: namely its supremely affordable MSRP and surprisingly deft sound.

Recent findings suggest that the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is $119 at Amazon U.S. and £119 at Amazon U.K. — this is incredibly cheap for a soundbar, let alone a soundbar that sounds this good. And, it's down to $74 for Black Friday.

I’ve also tested the $67 Majority Naga 60 and the $119 Sony HT-S100F, but I’d recommend the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar over both of these due to its superior bass.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

It has been revealed that now, let’s get one thing straight. The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar will not, and does not, sound like its more expensive brethren. Want Sonos Ray ($219) or Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen ($299) quality? It’s not here.

However, this is an $119 soundbar. That’s it. For the price of a monthly cellphone bill, you get a soundbar. And while it doesn’t have the same detail or controlled bass you’d expect on a premium model, that’s okay. That’s not what the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is, and that’s fine.

Even so, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar still sounds better than TV speakers — and that’s all it’s trying to be.

I always test soundbars with 4K Blu-rays, basic-tier Netflix, and music via Bluetooth or AirPlay (connectivity dependent). To test the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, I watched “Top Gun: Maverick,” “K-Pop Demon Hunters” and “The Batman” on 4K Blu-ray.

“Top Gun: Maverick”’is opening scene is a goldmine for speaker testing. There are all these different sounds fighting for attention: the iconic pulsing bassline in “Danger Zone,” high-frequency in-scene effects like whooshing ropes and clinking metal, and overpowering sounds like jet engines taking off.

According to recent reports, I could hear the propulsive bass in “Danger Zone,” which didn’t overpower the jet engines. While there was a little tinniness at the top of the high-end, I really didn’t mind this in the grand scheme of things. The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar performed admirably.

Dialogue was also clear, even in radioed dialogue scenes. While deep voices, like Tom Cruise’s, caused a little rumbling, I could still understand all dialogue.

In a recent development, “KPop Demon Hunters” also sounded strong: despite a little tinniness in some of the in-movie songs’ percussion, dialogue was particularly exceptional. Bass in the soundtrack was powerful, and diegetic sounds like slamming doors came through well.

According to recent reports, afterwards, I watched “The Batman,” which is a challenging movie for soundbars thanks to the moody dialogue and near-constant rainfall. I could hear every word muttered (yes, muttered; that’s how everyone speaks in this movie). Even footsteps across rainy concrete came through clearly.

Recent findings suggest that however, loud scenes — like the club scene — pushed dialogue to the back and overpowered the in-scene electronic music, which meant I strained to hear a few of the Penguin’s words. However, I didn’t experience this in any other movie. It’s a Batman thing.

I was extremely surprised and intrigued by this sound quality. It’s miles better than I thought it would be.

The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar has a range of EQ modes: dialogue, movie, music, and you can individually adjust bass. I had to cycle through the EQs to activate each EQ.

However, the EQs actually improved my viewing experience. I switched between “dialogue” and “movie” while watching “Top Gun”; movie increased bass; dialogue — ever-so surprisingly — clarified dialogue. Music made speech a little too sharp, but obviously, watching a movie in “music” mode is very much "play stupid games, win stupid prizes".

You can even listen to music via Bluetooth, but I wouldn’t write home about this. It would do in a pinch, but the percussion was tinny and the soundbar narrowed the soundstage. It’s fine, but I would just listen to music on one of the best speakers, like the JBL Flip 7.

It’s great to have these options on such a budget-friendly soundbar.

There’s very little I dislike about this soundbar, hence the 4.5-star rating.

I feel almost unfair marking this as a con, but Amazon kind of brought it upon itself by giving the soundbar DTS Virtual:X and Dolby Audio. There is no Dolby Atmos or any kind of surround sound. You only really find DTS Virtual:X on select DVDs, so you’ll need to ensure you buy compatible discs to really benefit from this.

Industry observers note that dolby Atmos content — like premium Netflix or Disney+ — will not play as true surround sound because the soundbar is physically incapable of it. If you want spatial audio, you'll have to go for the slightly more expensive Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus.

This is an incredibly cheap soundbar. I really don’t know how Amazon is making a profit on it, if it is at all. At $119, there’s really not much competition.

According to recent reports, the only soundbar that comes close is the $119 Sony HT-S100F, which is one of the best cheap soundbars on the market. However, the Sony’s bass is a little lackluster. While the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar’s bass can be a little rumbly at times, at least it isn’t lackluster. What you prefer will depend on you.

It has been revealed that in terms of similarly priced competition… well, that’s kind of it. I’ve also tested the Majority Naga 60, which is incredibly cheap at $67, but it can suffer from pinchy treble and rattling bass.

If you want better-than-TV-speaker sound on a serious budget, there’s only one answer to this question: Yes. Actually, wait, I’ve just thought of another: Heck yes.

Sources indicate that I was extremely surprised by the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar’s sound, and I’m sure you will be, too. After testing some disappointing and overpriced Amazon Fire Ember TVs, I wasn’t expecting much — but the soundbar completely blew me away. It’s room-filling, mostly well-controlled, and has extremely intelligible dialogue.

Sources indicate that it's much better than the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus ($139 on Amazon), whose built-in subwoofer overpowers dialogue in action-heavy scenes. If you have a little more to spend, you might want to look into the Amazon Fire TV Plus with Subwoofer ($229) or the model with Rears ($349).

However, for those on a serious budget, this is the best option out there. Hands-down.

Gemini Notebook's Latest Interactive Site Builder Is Much More Useful Than I Expected

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses.
  • That might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code.
  • Recent findings suggest that website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all customers, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something newly introduced. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

That might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

Recent findings suggest that website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all customers, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app. You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

Industry observers note that to make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

Sources indicate that with a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but says you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection.".

The finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a new window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

Recent findings suggest that for something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

Maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a major family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a newly introduced website.

It has been revealed that bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

It looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (410 w)

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Github ↗ Open Full Page

Fast-Anything: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (410 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, don't rewrite it in Rust.
  • Sources indicate that rewriting a whole app in Rust costs months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of target/.
  • fast-anything finds those functions, has your coding agent port only them to Rust, proves the port gives the same results on real recorded calls, and swaps it in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow.

Sources indicate that rewriting a whole app in Rust costs months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of target/. Most of the runtime sits in a few functions anyway.

fast-anything finds those functions, has your coding agent port only them to Rust, proves the port gives the same results on real recorded calls, and swaps it in. One command, fully reversible.

Ports are compiled with your Rust toolchain (rustup).

--agent takes claude, codex, or any command that reads a prompt on stdin. Without it, hand TASK.md to whatever you use.

That port looked right but compared bytes instead of characters. 148 of 500 real calls caught it. On top of the recorded calls, fast-anything derives extra cases and lets the original answer them: edge cases (NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, zero and ±1, non-ASCII text, empty and up to 16× bigger inputs) and shrunk inputs (tiny and random slices). Nothing is enabled until every case matches: same values (floats within 1e-9), errors where the original errors. A port that is right but slower per call than the original (calling into Rust costs more than the work saved) isn't enabled either. FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1 runs the original any time.

Real runs on an i5-10500, Windows 11 (C and C++: a 4-core GitHub Actions Linux runner). Reproduce them from examples/.

It has been revealed that fast-anything ports the outermost loop it can, not the tiny function called inside it, so the app crosses into Rust once instead of millions of times. Porting only the inner levenshtein gave 35× and 1.9×.

Industry observers note that it ports top-level, deterministic functions that take plain data (numbers, strings, lists, dicts, typed arrays…), including ones in your entry script when its main code sits under if __name__ == "__main__": (or if __FILE__ == $0, or if (import.meta.main) / if (require.main === module)). In Python that means module-level functions and @staticmethods, in Java, C# and PHP static methods (and PHP functions), in Go plain functions, in C and C++ free functions and static methods. scan indicates why anything else can't move yet.

Sources indicate that ruby, Java, Go, PHP, C, C++ and C# need no headers, bindings or extra tools: the port is a plain Rust library with one C entry point taking and returning JSON, and fast-anything replays the recorded calls against it directly. Any language that can call C can use that bridge.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after releasing developer beta 2 of macOS 27.3 earlier this week, the firm is now rolling out the public beta for owners looking to try the latest features ahead of next month’s official release. Here’s what’s coming.

Last Monday, Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 2, with upcoming privacy controls for Full Disk Access and automation tools, and the availability of Apple Intelligence in China.

Those came alongside several upcoming features and tools on macOS 27.3 beta 1, including vertical tabs and adaptive dark mode in Safari, native Live Activities support, Markdown rendering in Quick Look, additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through iCloud links, and Siri AI support for Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

And speaking of Siri AI, macOS 27.3 also expands the assistant’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing consumers to perform more complex actions in Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders. Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to build more advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions.

While macOS 27.2 was a rather uneventful revision, macOS 27.3 is shaping up to be the biggest update since the release of macOS 27, and consumers on the public beta can now try out these new features ahead of their official release.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 2 is 26C5047e, which matches the developer build.

If you’d like to join Apple’s free public beta program, visit beta.apple.com.

In a recent development, did you spot anything fresh in today’s beta? Let us know in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The BBC has apologized to viewers after lewd noises could be heard during the Strictly Come Dancing live show at Blackpool’s Tower Ballroom.

A recording of sex noises appeared to be played from the audience as Strictly judge Motsi Mabuse delivered her remarks about the performance of Delta Goodrem and partner Kai Widdrington.

Microphones picked up the noise. Mabuse turned to the audience to establish what was going on, before facing the camera again and exclaiming: “It’s not me.”.

Emma Willis had to apologise at the end of tonight’s Strictly Come Dancing for ‘anything offensive’ that was heard during the show. Turns out, it was sex noises played by someone in the background. The episode of #Strictly is right now still not available on iPlayer. pic.twitter.com/fPxDW45h1V.

At the end of the show (the format on which ABC’s Dancing with the Stars is based), presenter Emma Willis apologized to viewers “if you heard any audio disruptions”. Industry observers note that the police were called to the incident. A Lancashire Police spokesperson told The Guardian: “We are aware of an incident that took place during the filming of Strictly Come Dancing in Blackpool.

“We have been in contact with the event organisers, and a formal complaint has been made to us. A mobile phone has been seized and we are now looking into the matter to see if any criminal offences have taken place.”.

Recent findings suggest that it is the second time a BBC live show has been interrupted by sex noises. Coverage of an FA Cup tie between Wolves and Liverpool was plagued by an apparent pornography prank in 2023.

Gary Lineker was anchoring live build-up to the replay match at the Molineux Stadium when he was interrupted by what sounded like sex noises coming from the studio.

The former England player looked perplexed by the noise in the studio, joking to fellow presenter Alan Shearer: “I don’t know who’s making that noise … It’s toasty in this studio, it’s a bit noisy as well. I don’t know if somebody is sending something on someone’s phone, if it’s a joke. I don’t know whether you heard it at home.”.

Lineker later tweeted a picture of a phone, which he stated had been taped to the back of the set in an apparent act of sabotage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other shows dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

Recent findings suggest that this time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

According to recent reports, situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that when pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

According to recent reports, A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

Sources indicate that A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Sources indicate that mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that rapidly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

In a recent development, peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

The fresh Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

Four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

You can spend plenty of time getting your Mac, display, and desk just right. But what about the chair you use every day? Between typing, taking video calls, and leaning back to watch something, your position changes throughout the day. Your chair should be able to keep up.

That’s the idea behind LiberNovo’s ergonomic chairs, which combine support that moves with you and a choice of sizes, including the Maxis range for bigger and taller people. For Black Friday, LiberNovo is taking up to 42% off in the U.S., with chairs starting at $609 and offers running November 19–30.

According to recent reports, adjusting a chair for your desk is one thing. Keeping that support as you change position is another. LiberNovo’s Dynamic Support System links the neck support, backrest, armrests, and seat so they move together as you recline.

The Bionic FlexFit Backrest adds eight flexible panels that contour independently. Rather than relying on a single rigid backrest, the design lets different sections follow your back as you shift or turn. Once you’ve adjusted the chair to fit, the system is designed to maintain contact through those movements with fewer manual readjustments.

Both the Omni and Maxis families offer five recline positions: 105, 115, 125, 135, and 160 degrees. That gives you options for desk work, a more relaxed position for watching a video, and a deeper recline for a break.

Industry observers note that A higher weight limit is only part of finding a chair that fits. Taller owners also need enough seat depth, a headrest that reaches the right spot, and armrests with room to adjust.

Industry observers note that the LiberNovo Maxis range addresses those details with a 52 cm seat depth, a wider backrest with a flared base, and an extended-travel headrest with 140 mm of vertical adjustment and 120 mm of front-to-back adjustment. Its armrests sit lower and offer a wider, longer adjustment range to accommodate larger builds.

According to recent reports, liberNovo recommends Maxis for people approximately 5 feet 10 inches to 6 feet 7 inches tall, with a maximum supported weight of 399 pounds. Maxis is certified to BIFMA X5.11. The seat cushion uses firmer support at the rear and a softer front edge, while a six-spring Controlled Recline System is designed to build resistance progressively as you lean back.

In a recent development, for a shallower seat, the Omni family offers 45 cm and 48 cm configurations. Choosing between the two families starts with fit, then comes down to which features you want.

There are three feature tiers in each family. Omni SE and Maxis Manual offer manually adjusted lumbar support, without a motor or battery. Both retain the flexible backrest, dynamic support, and five recline positions.

The Maxis Electric includes motorized lumbar adjustment and OmniStretch, a five-minute powered stretch sequence used in deep recline.

Recent findings suggest that omni Pro and Maxis Airflow add Active AirFlow seat ventilation. A fan draws air through the cushion to carry heat away, and an occupancy sensor pauses the fan when you stand up. These models also include a larger 3,000 mAh rechargeable battery.

LiberNovo’s warranty covers the frame and structural components for six years, and electronic components for two years.

#108368. Industry News: If You Loved 'Yellowjackets,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (985 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: If You Loved 'Yellowjackets,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying.
  • Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.
  • The survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yellowjackets is a vibe. The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying. The dual timelines build tension around the story’s many mysteries, and the complex characters (no one’s completely good or evil on this show) make for a lot of surprising plot swerves that feel grounded despite the supernatural implications all around them. If you’re looking for more of that specific flavor of horror, you should probably watch Alive.

Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.

The survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances. They use the wrecked plane as shelter in the withering cold, they scavenge for anything that could be useful, and they ration out the only food they have: Some chocolates and a case of wine. But an early mistake leaves them without any food at all, and slowly they come to the sickening realization that their best chance at survival is to treat the corpses of their friends and families scattered around the crash site as a food source.

There’s no supernatural aspect, but the story has a similar tone of desperation and despair as Yellowjackets. These are people determined to survive in an impossible situation, and they do things that no one outside of their shared experience could possibly understand. The real-life origins of the story add a sense of horror that more than matches the fictional “It” that haunts the girls of Yellowjackets; putting yourself into that very real experience makes it clear just how terrified everyone was. Rent Alive on Prime Video.

If you’re craving more cannibals, cults, and crazies at the mercy of nature itself, here are a few more movies you should check out.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to watch a movie that is essentially an adaptation of Yellowjackets, check out Eden. Even though it was released years before the show, the stories are so similar (albeit largely gender-flipped) that the producers of Eden actually sued, claiming plagiarism (they lost). In the film, a men’s soccer team (and two women on the same plane) crash-land on a deserted island, and as they fight for survival, things descend into, yes, madness and cannibalism as the survivors suffer dwindling food and water supplies and the rise of two violently opposed factions. It’s not nearly as deeply imagined as Yellowjackets, and it doesn’t have the supernatural hints of the show, but if you want a truly similar story, it’s a good choice. Stream Eden on The Roku Channel, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that you obviously cannot discuss Yellowjackets without discussing Lord of the Flies, William Golding’s 1954 novel about a group of schoolboys who descend into brutality and savagery when they’re stranded on a deserted island. The book has been adapted many times, but the 1963 version directed by Peter Brook is still the best version. Brook managed to elicit remarkably naturalistic performances from his young actors, giving the story a realistic tone that is somehow more terrifying than any amount of horror vibes. Stream Lord of the Flies on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

A slower and more haunting story, Picnic at Hanging Rock explores some of the same themes as Yellowjackets in an entirely different way. On Valentine’s Day in the year 1900, several students and teachers from an all-girls private school in Victoria, Australia, head to Hanging Rock for a picnic. Four students head off to explore and fall inexplicably asleep, and then three vanish, along with one of the teachers. Dreamy and drenched in dread, the story never offers any easy answers, and it explores themes of invading natural areas where you’re not wanted, burgeoning (and confusing) adolescent sexuality, and how our fear of the unknowable warps our perspective and often diminishes our humanity. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, you can never really go wrong with a Hitchcock film, and if you’re looking for another story about a disparate group of people forced to make terrifying decisions in order to survive, watch Lifeboat (based on a story by John Steinbeck). One of the director’s most underrated films, it’s the story of a group of survivors in a lifeboat after a German U-boat sinks their ship during World War II (including one survivor from the German boat). It’s a masterful suspense engine that’s not afraid to have its characters discuss the moral and ethical quandaries facing them as they struggle to survive and maintain their humanity under a constant threat of death. Stream Lifeboat on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

If you love the supernatural aspects of Yellowjackets as the girls come to believe a force they call “It” is out in the woods, check out The Ritual. Four friends embark on a hike in the wilds of northern Sweden to honor their deceased friend. When one of them is injured, they leave the marked trail to take a shortcut through the forest—where they are soon forced to shelter in an abandoned cabin, just like the Yellowjackets—and things begin to slide into the terrifying when they encounter a cult worshipping an ancient deity that grants them immortality in exchange for human sacrifices. It’s as if the show was condensed to an hour-and-a-half and the terror quotient was turned way, way up. Stream The Ritual on Netflix.
