It has been revealed that “The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

Industry observers note that one way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

Industry observers note that in Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company confirmed a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main concern is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

Recent findings suggest that not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

In a recent development, “A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the organization believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.

The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” claims Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

Sources indicate that lightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to promptly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

According to recent reports, lightSolver’s team is at the moment working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the organization’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

It has been revealed that yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” Upcoming indicates. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick Latest, Optalysis.

It has been revealed that instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

According to recent reports, some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

According to recent reports, fresh states that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

According to recent reports, how likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he states. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

In a recent development, however, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Indicates Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

In a recent development, whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” notes Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

It has been revealed that I’ve used Apple’s Calendar app for years, and there’s an elegant simplicity to it. But one key area the app has long lagged behind competitors is event creation.

When you need to create a new event, the Calendar app historically has required manually filling in various fields for the title, date, time, invitees, etc. By contrast, the excellent third-party app Fantastical lets you type in natural language and it automatically fills in relevant parameters based on what you type.

It has been revealed that in iOS 27, Apple finally introduces its own natural language input for Calendar events. You can type out your event details and certain recognized parameters will be used to automatically fill in the detail fields.

While the feature still isn’t on par with what Fantastical offers, since it doesn’t support as many data points as the third-party alternative, it’s very much a step in the right direction.

Apple has always pitched Siri as being like a personal assistant. As such, calendar-related tasks should have been Siri’s strong suit. But until iOS 27, you couldn’t actually manage your calendar very well using Siri.

With Siri AI, that’s changed in a massive way. Now, you can do things like:.

One of my favorite personal examples is from this summer when the NFL schedule was released. I asked Siri to find the Dallas Cowboys schedule and add every game to my calendar, and it pulled this off with ease.

Siri is so much better than before at assisting with your calendar, and iOS 27.3 will bring even more capabilities soon.

Quality sleep and back pain do not go hand in hand, but a comfortable mattress that relieves discomfort can make a huge difference to how well you sleep at night. The best mattresses for back pain that we've tested are often specialist beds been engineered to support the spine and reduce lumbar pressure. But as our team of testers have discovered first hand, many of the best mattresses you can buy online also boast excellent lumbar support.

It has been revealed that below, we've selected four beds that fit the specific criteria we recommend for high levels of comfort and support when you have back pain. Even better, there are excellent Black Friday mattress deals on each of them. Let's take a look...

Our Helix Midnight Luxe review score: ★★★★User score: ★★★★½ (9,800+ reviews).

The Rx is our top recommendation for anyone living with significant back or joint conditions, such as scoliosis or sciatica. The current Saatva Black Friday deal shaves a hefty $425 off all sizes of the RX with our semi-exclusive link, bringing queen down to $3,214 (was $3,639). It comes with a year's trial, lifetime warranty, and free white glove delivery.

Our Saatva Rx review score: ★★★★½User score: ★★★★★ (600+ reviews).

We found it to be a good choice for side and lighter weight back sleepers, but too plush for stomach sleepers. It also comes with a year's sleep trial and limited lifetime warranty.

Our Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Essential review score: ★★★½User score: ★★★★½ (800+ reviews).

According to recent reports, this double-sided ultra-firm mattress offers a reassuringly sturdy sleep surface, delivering exceptional top-to-toe support. Our Plank Firm review score: ★★★★User score: ★★★★½.

For a mattress to be considered a good option for anyone with back pain, it needs to perform well in three specific areas; pressure relief, temperature regulation, and edge support.

In a recent development, in order to select only the beds that offer meaningful relief to people with a bad back, we've combed our test data to ensure each of the mattresses featured here have scored a minimum of 3.5 out of 5 in our pressure relief, temperature and edge support tests. Here's how the Helix Midnight Luxe, Saatva Rx, Plank Firm and Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Essential performed and compare across these crucial metrics:.

Pressure relief score (out of 5).

Temperature regulation: Reliable temperature regulation is an vital feature of a mattress for back pain. Waking up hot and sweaty can lead to more movement (like kicking off the covers), which can cause further injury. Pressure relief: This is a term to describe how much cushioning there is along the touch points of the mattress. For example, for side sleepers, this will be your shoulders, hips and knees. For back sleepers, this will likely be your lumbar region and upper back and shoulders. Minimal pressure relief can lead to a build-up of pressure, which can exacerbate existing pain. Edge Support: This describes how sturdy a mattress is at its edges and corners. This is an important feature for any mattress, but especially those with back pain who may need to sit comfortably and safely before standing.

Recent findings suggest that the Helix Midnight Luxe is superbly comfortable for side sleepers, and it's also an excellent choice for those with lower and upper back pain, as well as hip pain. As a luxury hotel-style hybrid, it is a premium mattress. However, a current 25% sale means you can buy a queen Midnight Luxe for $1,874 at Helix. The pillow top is crafted from high density foam which cushions the shoulders hips and knees, but also keeps the spine in healthy alignment while sleeping. This high density foam also works to gently cradle the lumbar region, which is the 'S' shape of your back. Underpinning this support are up to 1,000 individually wrapped coils that prevent the hips from sinking. Our lead tester, who has experienced recurrent lower back pain for the past decade, felt none of the pain she usually experiences while sleeping on the Luxe. Temperature wise, our test data mirrored our real life experience. It's a breathable bed with reliably sturdy edges for sitting on before standing.The Luxe is accredited by the American Chiropractic Association and is a great fit for aches and pains. However, those with more pronounced back pain have the option to upgrade to ErgoAlign. This is a layer of denser foam around the mid-section, bolstering support in this area. Luxe is a great option for side and back sleeper with back ache but for significant back pain, we recommend the Saatva Rx below.

In a recent development, the Saatva Rx is our top recommendation for those living with significant back or joint conditions, such as sciatica or arthritis. It's an ACA accredited specialist mattress, and it's priced accordingly (it's $3,214 for a queen at Saatva in this year's Saatva Black Friday sale). A large part of what sets the Rx apart from other back pain beds pain is its Therapeutic Support Core. This is made up of the brand’s proprietary Wave-Tech Foam and individually wrapped coils for support, cradling the spine in all sleep positions. Above that, a layer of micro-coils sandwiched between two slabs of high-density foam and a strip of gel-infused memory foam provides soothing support along the lumbar.Saatva rates the Rx as 'Supportive Plush' but our experience of sleeping on it was that it errs on the firmer side, making it a more comfortable choice for back and stomach sleepers. It's still comfy for side sleepers, but our lead tester — who has mild scoliosis — felt her spine was better supported when sleeping on her back. For general aches and pains, we recommend the (slightly cheaper) Saatva Classic Mattress instead, which does an excellent job of soothing mild back and hip pain.

Industry observers note that it's a common misconception that people with back pain need a solid mattress. However, some people simply prefer the feel of a firm bed. And at 30% off for Black Friday, a queen Plank Firm is $1,025.50 at Plank, which is excellent value for money on this top rated firm mattress.The Plank Firm is a dual-sided all foam mattress rated as Firm on one side and Extra Firm on the other. It's been crafted from the inside out, where 6" of high density foam underpins the unyielding sleep surface. Regardless of how you flip it, make no mistake, this is a firm mattress. With its 2" top layer of comfort foam which provides cushioning around the touch points of the bed, the Firm side will have wider appeal. However, with just 0.75" slither of comfort foam, the Extra Firm side feels reassuringly solid for those who want to keep their spine in healthy alignment when sleeping on their stomach.It's accredited by the ACA and boasts superb motion isolation, which is good news for bed sharers. It's also nice and sturdy around the edge. However, with a score of 3.5 out of 5 for temperature control, it just scrapes through our benchmark of being temperature regulating enough for it to be considered a good choice for back pain. For hot sleepers, we recommend upgrading to the GlacioTex cooling layer.

Sources indicate that in a mattress for back pain guide featuring ACA accredited beds with zoned lumbar support, you might be wondering why we have added the Essential to the mix, a mattress that at $489.30 for a queen at Brooklyn Bedding costs a fraction of the price and boasts none of those things.That's because, when combing our test data, it became apparent that the Essential performs well enough in crucial areas (temperature regulation, edge support and pressure relief) to make it a good choice for side sleepers looking for cushioning around their shoulders and hips, without sacrificing healthy spinal alignment. It's supportive enough for lighter weight back sleepers, but heavier bodies with need something sturdier to prevent their hips from sinking in this position. The Essential comes in 5 different heights ranging from 6"to 14" and we tested the 10". Increasing the height will likely mean increasing the support... and also the price. For a sturdier all foam mattress for back sleeping within a similar price range, we would opt for the Siena Signature. It scored 3.3 out of 5 for temperature regulation but is a fantastic budget friendly, firmer choice. For ACA accreditation, enhanced cooling and zoned lumbar support, we recommend the Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Pro Hybrid, a mid-range marvel coming in at under $1,000 for a queen in the Brooklyn Bedding mattress sales.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Popular secure messaging app Signal has rolled out a upcoming update that automatically disables screenshots for the sake of blocking Siri AI from reading your chats. Here are the details.

Signal’s latest app enhancement on iPhone disables a key system feature: taking screenshots.

As Signal told Reuters, that’s because Apple doesn’t at the moment provide better tools for iOS developers to safeguard app content from Siri AI and third-party AI agents.

By default, people who update and try to take a screenshot will see a message that states: “Screenshot prevented by ‘Block Siri AI’ setting.”.

Fortunately, there’s an easy workaround. Users who want to re-enable screenshots can do so by visiting Signal’s privacy settings and turning off the new toggle that’s labeled ‘Block Siri AI.’.

Here’s 9to5Mac’s own Arin Waichulis:.

Signal now blocks in-app screenshots on iPhone to keep Siri AI from reading chatsIt’s a new toggle in settings that’s on by default, but can be turned offNo equivalent for its Mac app pic.twitter.com/ImsinqMNPq.

Here’s exactly what that toggle does, per the in-app settings:.

Prevent Siri AI from scanning Signal content. This will also block you from taking screenshots in the app and App Switcher.

It’s good to see that consumers can manually disable the fresh privacy setting if they want. But Signal’s decision to block screenshots does raise important questions about the potential gap in privacy tools for iOS developers.

Industry observers note that apple already lets you block Siri AI from accessing whichever apps you manually exclude, and that became even easier in iOS 27.2. But rather than directing customers to that system option, Signal seems to believe it needed to take action itself with this update.

What do you think of Signal’s latest move? Let us know in the comments.

  • Anduril founder Palmer Luckey speaks at Space Systems Command, Los Angeles Air Force Base, El Segundo, 6 August 2026.

  • “The US government isn’t even willing to stand up for Ukraine because they’re afraid of losing their constellation,” Luckey said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anduril founder Palmer Luckey speaks at Space Systems Command, Los Angeles Air Force Base, El Segundo, 6 August 2026.

Palmer Luckey says the US government will not let Ukraine use Starshield, because it fears Russia would destroy it. Starshield is the Pentagon’s military satellite network, and SpaceX helps run it. The Anduril founder made the case to Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday.

“The US government isn’t even willing to stand up for Ukraine because they’re afraid of losing their constellation,” Luckey said.

Sources indicate that he was defending Elon Musk, who spoke later that day and accused Zelenskyy of lying about Starshield speed limits. Luckey noted he likes Musk personally, so people should take his view “with a pound of salt”.

His argument ran like this. Russia has hinted that it could destroy the civilian Starlink network if Ukraine keeps using it for attacks. The same satellites that cover Ukraine also orbit over the US. So Musk should not have to risk his whole network when Washington will not risk its own, Luckey remarked.

Industry observers note that “Nobody in the West actually wants Ukraine to win. They just want them to not lose for as long as possible, which is a bizarre and absurd warfighting position,” he said.

According to recent reports, luckey stated he fully supports Ukraine, and that Anduril has worked there since the second day of the war. Who America sells weapons to is not his call, he added.

“I’m a dog on a chain and I need to be kept that way,” Luckey said.

Luckey co-leads Project Meridian, the Pentagon’s 120-day study of future war, with Musk and Newt Gingrich. He said it looks at what war could look like in 2050, and that the MITRE Corporation runs it. The group met at Cheyenne Mountain the day before. It agreed to focus on ideas that have no champion in the Pentagon.

According to recent reports, one example is weather control, he remarked, such as changing where rain falls at sea so forces get a clearer view of targets. He also took credit for pushing the Trump administration to rename the Defense Department the Department of War.

Industry observers note that sorkin read him a criticism from Wes Bryant, who until last year ran the Pentagon’s assessment of civilian harm. Bryant called Meridian a sign of oligarchy in government. Luckey stated more than 20 people sit on it, including retired generals and admirals. Nobody attacked Eric Schmidt for joining the Defense Innovation Board under Joe Biden, he said, and the report will be public.

Luckey wants the US to resume nuclear testing, mainly to see what an electromagnetic pulse does to modern electronics. The models used today were built for transistors thousands of times larger than those in a phone, he said. He is not confident his own systems would survive, even when built to the hardening rules.

“They were designed for the type of cell phone that Abraham Lincoln would have used,” he stated.

He stated no AI model can be controlled, because every major model has been jailbroken within months. Data centres can still be shut off, he added. The AI in weapons is a different technology from chatbots, he argued, and more reliable than the older seekers it replaces.

“I am way more afraid of the civilian collateral side for dumb weapons than I am for smart weapons,” Luckey said.

Sources indicate that some companies have used chatbots for targeting and made mistakes, he said, without naming them. China wants Jensen Huang out of Nvidia, he said, so he wants him back. Luckey still opposes selling chips to China.

Industry observers note that luckey also defended public executions. The state should rarely use the death penalty, he stated. When it does, it should do so in public and without medical cover, so people can judge whether it got it right.

Industry observers note that “Executions should be brutal. They should be violent,” he mentioned.

He closed on his 2017 firing from Facebook, after he gave $9,000 to a pro-Trump group. He blames former Oculus colleagues, not Mark Zuckerberg, and now works with Meta on a combat headset for the US Army.

“It’s probably better for everybody that I got fired, but I have not let it go,” Luckey mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that my sleep debt has coincided with a series of 3 a.m. wake ups (something else the Oura Ring tracks), and a general feeling of low energy. I've been a bit bleh, you might say. I'd assumed the season change was to blame but now I recognize the problem is lying in my sleep. And that's something I can fix.

Having identified my increasing sleep debt and subsequent lethargy are related to a series of late night wake ups, I know I need to change my wind-down routine. Thanks to the Oura Ring's hidden body clock feature, which uses my natural circadian rhythm to send me bedtime reminders, I now know when to start my night-time routine. (That's more warm evening showers, dimming the lights, and swapping my sudden interest in Sudoko for puzzles I'm actually good at. ).

Industry observers note that and it's paying off. Last night I enjoyed an impressive 1 hour and 32 minutes off deep sleep, alongside 93% sleep efficiency. Hopefully it shouldn't take long repay my sleep debt entirely.

Latest Update: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • Industry observers note that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • These ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

Industry observers note that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash fresh competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is notable because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The manufacturer’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company declared a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

In a recent development, such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s right now receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.Penny Gray PhotographyObjection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Industry observers note that finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

According to recent reports, pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s at the moment receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

In a recent development, but this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

Recent findings suggest that we cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s key to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky promptly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a fresh instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

In a recent development, these examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

Recent findings suggest that in the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

It has been revealed that consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its customers because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

Industry observers note that the implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Industry observers note that even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

Sources indicate that this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

Sources indicate that what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

A real Linux kernel, compiled to WebAssembly

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A real Linux kernel, compiled to WebAssembly.
  • Try it · Performance · Features · CLI · How it works · Benchmarks · JavaScript SDK.
  • Industry observers note that unkernel is Linux 7.x built as a single wasm module with a real MMU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A real Linux kernel, compiled to WebAssembly. It boots to a shell in less than a second.

Try it · Performance · Features · CLI · How it works · Benchmarks · JavaScript SDK.

Industry observers note that unkernel is Linux 7.x built as a single wasm module with a real MMU. The kernel (syscalls, scheduler, memory management, ext4, TCP/IP) is compiled code, not emulated, so programs get Linux's own behavior down to the edge cases. Only user programs are emulated: unmodified aarch64 (arm64) Linux binaries, so Alpine and Debian packages run as they are.

Open a page and you have a Linux machine with a shell, a package manager, a persistent disk, internet access, and a screen with sound. It runs entirely on your device, with nothing to install and no server, and every layer is open source. How it works explains the design.

Much of what makes a system feel slow lives in the kernel: starting processes, syscalls, page faults, file and network I/O. In unkernel that path runs at wasm speed.

Recent findings suggest that the syscall and fork numbers were measured on 2026-11-14 (with the riscv64 user space the project started with; the path through the kernel is the same), the JIT numbers on 2026-11-18. CPU-heavy programs are well behind native: apk search over the main index takes about 0.8 s, apk add python3 about 3.4 s. Benchmarks has the full numbers.

Anything a program relies on, from /proc and epoll to cgroups and overlayfs, behaves as it does on a server, because it runs the same code.

Known limits lists what is still missing.

Open unkernel.dev. A shell appears after a download of about 10 MB. Your changes are saved in the browser, and the status icon opens options, diagnostics, and export or reset for your disk. Ctrl-A n (or ⌘A n on a Mac) or + on the status line opens another terminal window with its own shell, up to 9; Ctrl-A and a digit switches.

The page takes a few URL parameters:.

In a recent development, browsers can't open raw TCP sockets, so the page reaches the internet through a Wisp proxy. The default one accepts only known origins, so if you host the page somewhere else, point ?wisp= at your own proxy.

This boots Alpine, with networking over your host's sockets. Press Ctrl-] to quit. The package holds the kernel and a small base system; the first run downloads the Alpine image (about 4 MB) from the GitHub release of your version and keeps it in ~/.cache/unkernel.

It has been revealed that without --data, changes to the root file system are kept in memory and gone at exit; with it, each distro keeps its own in /data/distros//. --distro also takes an image file or an http(s) URL, and UNKERNEL_CACHE_DIR moves the download cache.

Exit codes: 0 power off, 1 halt or boot failure, 2 restart, 124 timeout, 253 kernel panic, 254 wasm trap, 255 fatal error. The CLI is built on the JavaScript SDK: --mount uses its host mounts and --forward its vm.connect().

Most "Linux in the browser" projects take one of three approaches:.

unkernel keeps the best of each: the real Linux kernel, running at native wasm speed, under unmodified binaries with a real MMU.

The kernel is compiled straight to WebAssembly. User programs run on kwemu, an aarch64 CPU written in Zig and linked into the kernel. kwemu walks the kernel's own page tables, so memory management is done by the real Linux code.

When a program makes a syscall, kwemu returns to the kernel, which handles it as native wasm. There is no emulated trap and no emulated kernel mode in between. Task switches use JSPI (WebAssembly.Suspending), so the kernel gets real stacks that it can suspend and resume.

kwemu runs blocks of guest code decoded once into compact ops (what has no op runs through a reference interpreter), and hot user code goes through a second tier: a JIT that compiles those blocks to wasm modules at run time, with output that matches the interpreter bit for bit. Benchmarks shows what each tier costs.

Devices are small paravirtual drivers that talk to the JavaScript host: block (kwblk), network (kwnet, with a user-mode TCP/IP stack in JS), display, input and sound (kwfb, kwinput, kwsnd), vsock (kwvsock) and shared memory (kwshm).

The design helps most with syscalls. These were measured under Node:.

According to recent reports, in this test (2026-11-14) fork is faster than native. Pure computation is slower. kwemu's decoded-op interpreter runs integer code at about 250-300 million guest instructions per second under Node (2026-11-17), and the JIT makes real Alpine work 1.6 to 2.3 times as fast as that (2026-11-18: an ash loop 2.5 s against 4.0 s, seq 100000 | sort -r 3.1 s against 7.1 s, seq 250000 | gzip | gunzip 3.5 s against 6.5 s), which is still well behind native.

According to recent reports, importing unkernel picks the Node or browser entry automatically, and unkernel/node or unkernel/web selects one explicitly. The kernel ships in the package (unkernel/unkernel.wasm) and loads from next to the entry, streamed and compiled while it downloads. It carries a small base system that mounts a distro image read-only under an overlay root and runs its init; createKernel() without distro boots the base shell (busybox and unkernel's tools), which needs no download.

The distro images are not in the package. On Node, fetchDistro("alpine") (or "debian") downloads one once from the GitHub release of the package's version, checks it against the release's distros.json (size and SHA-256), keeps it in ~/.cache/unkernel (UNKERNEL_CACHE_DIR) and returns its path; nothing else in the SDK downloads anything. In the browser, host the image yourself (it is read lazily with range requests) and pass its URL:.

Changes to the root file system stay in memory, unless a persistent data disk (labelled kwdata) is attached: then each distro keeps them in /data/distros// on it.

Sources indicate that networking is off unless you pass net. Any object with connect and lookup methods can carry the guest's TCP and DNS, so you can write your own backend.

createImageFromKwsparse(file, template) makes a latest data disk from the template the kernel carries (bundledBoot(module).datadisk). In the browser, openHttpDisk(url) keeps your writes in IndexedDB and openDataDisk() gives you the persistent data disk that the page uses. Anything that implements BlockDevice works too, and a disk of your own can be the root: cmdline: "console=hvc0 root=/dev/wda rw" with initrd: null.

According to recent reports, exec() runs a program on pipes and resolves with { stdout, stderr, exitCode, signal }, also for a non-zero exit. Pass encoding: "buffer" for bytes, and cwd or env as you would to child_process. On the distro images programs run as the user user (uid 1000, in /home/user), who has sudo without a password; pass user: "root" (or another name or uid) to run as someone else. The base shell is root's.

spawn(file, args, { cols, rows }) runs a program on a pty, in the zigpty / node-pty shape, with resize(), kill(signal) and close() (a hangup). Run as many as you like. Keep reading output: the guest program waits while nobody does.

With pty: false the program gets pipes: stdin, stdout and stderr web streams, byte for byte.

A file system is a plain object tree (a function is a computed file, evaluated once per open), a MemoryFs you read and write from the host, nodeFs(dir), or your own Fs: getattr, readdir and open by path, sync or async, plus whichever change methods you want. Mounts are served over 9p on vsock. Each guest write reaches the host as it happens, and a host change shows in the guest within a second.

According to recent reports, these are byte streams with real flow control and no network in between. vsock is on unless you pass vsock: false.

According to recent reports, vm.connect(port) reaches a TCP server on the guest's loopback through the guest's kwtty, over vsock, so it needs no network. It resolves once the guest has connected (PtyError ECONNREFUSED if nothing listens) with readable and writable byte streams, half-close included, close() and closed. The CLI's --forward HOSTPORT:GUESTPORT uses it.

vm.fetch(url, init) sends an HTTP/1.1 request to a server in the guest and returns a Response whose body streams. It always connects to the guest's 127.0.0.1 at the URL's port; the host name only goes into the Host header, so vm.fetch("http://localhost:8000/") reaches a dev server listening on port 8000. fetchOver(connect, url, init) is the same client over any byte stream.

/dev/shm exists once the guest's init has mounted it, so wait for the guest before create() (an exec() waits for it). openId(id) opens a memfd that a guest program exported through /dev/kwshm. views() exists only when the kernel runs inline.

Industry observers note that evdev also has button(), move(), moveTo() and wheel() for a mouse or tablet. onInput tells you when a program opens the keyboard and mouse; until then, send keys to the console. readFrame() waits for a fresh frame.

The kernel runs in a worker thread or Web Worker, with the same API. Disks and the network are given as specs, which the worker builds: { kind: "file", path } on Node, { kind: "http", url } and { kind: "data", template: "bundled" } in browsers. Input and frames go through shared memory when it is available (vm.transport says). This mode is experimental.

An SMP kernel (a bundle with the SMP patch) boots on several CPUs with cpus: 4, each CPU in a thread of its own on one shared memory. In browsers that needs a cross-origin isolated page and worker: true, because a CPU blocks while it waits for another, which a page's main thread may not; webCpuBlocker() notes why it cannot, and vm.stats().cpus how many CPUs the kernel got.

Recent findings suggest that on a server, worker: true keeps the event loop free at no cost in speed, and cpus: 4 gets most of what more CPUs give (about 3x on parallel work; 8 or 16 add little, and each CPU adds to boot time and takes 9 MiB of guest memory). node test/profile.ts measures your host, and the page's /profile.html a browser.

The SDK has some limits, on top of the kernel's known limits. There is no guest agent beyond terminal sessions, so you drive the guest through a terminal or its console, or over vsock with your own program. stop() doesn't shut the guest down cleanly, so prefer poweroff. Only one kernel can run per thread. Types ship as .d.mts and use the DOM's WebAssembly types, so a Node-only TypeScript project needs "lib": ["dom"] or skipLibCheck.

It has been revealed that you need Linux (x86-64 or arm64), Zig 0.16, Node 24, clang 21+ with the wasm target, and the usual build tools. ./setup.sh --check lists what's missing. The first build takes about 12 minutes, most of it spent on a patched wasm-ld, and uses 5 GiB of disk.

The build makes the kernel bundle vendor/build/bundle/unkernel.wasm and the distro images vendor/build/distro/{alpine,debian}.erofs with their index distros.json; a source checkout uses those and never downloads them. guest/README.md describes the base system and how to add a distro.

In a recent development, kernel/README.md maps the kernel directory and its build steps. AGENTS.md and .agents/ hold the contributor notes: the kernel, its devices and the guest image, invariants, workflows, which tests to run, and the roadmap.

Made with ♥ by Pooya Parsa (pi0), sponsored by ▲ Vercel.

Sources indicate that everything is open source: the kernel patches, the emulator and its JIT, the patched linker, the SDK and the page. ./setup.sh rebuilds the kernel file from source.

According to recent reports, the project is GPL-2.0-or-later (LICENSE) unless a file indicates otherwise. The JavaScript SDK and page (js/, web/, SDK tests) are MIT (LICENSE-MIT), so you can embed them anywhere.

It has been revealed that the npm package ships a Linux kernel (GPL-2.0) with a small base system (Alpine's static busybox, GPL-2.0, and unkernel's own tools), so it is MIT AND GPL-2.0-only. The distro images it downloads hold the distributions' packages, which keep their own licenses. The kernel's source is Linux 7.3.4 plus kernel/patches/linux (arch/wasm is based on linux-wasm's). Those patches and kernel/tools/fake-llvm are GPL-2.0-only, and the patches in kernel/patches/llvm follow LLVM's license (Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception).

iOS 27 gives the Messages app a variety of welcome upgrades, including one I’ve found myself using a lot: a Smart Reply feature that’s now personalized to the user’s writing style.

When the first wave of Apple Intelligence features were unveiled in 2024, one that I immediately thought sounded useful was Smart Reply.

Industry observers note that the idea behind Smart Reply is simple. Rather than needing to manually type out replies in Messages and Mail, your iPhone can offer prewritten replies you can choose and send with a couple taps.

Great in theory, but the ‘Smart’ part of Smart Reply struggled to materialize in iOS 18.

According to recent reports, fortunately, with a key Apple Intelligence upgrade in iOS 27, the latest version of the feature finally lives up to its name. Per Apple:.

Smart Reply in Mail and Messages can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.

Before, Smart Reply would look at the context of a conversation to craft its suggestions. But now, it also aims to match your writing style, punctuation, and tone.

In iOS 18, I almost never used Smart Reply. That’s because despite being fine at suggesting replies that technically worked, those suggestions didn’t sound like me at all.

In a recent development, that’s changed in iOS 27. Smart Reply now consistently impresses me. It no longer offers generic responses that sound like AI wrote them. Instead, its suggestions actually fit with my normal style of communication.

Industry observers note that the only drawback is that right now, you’ll only ever see two Smart Reply suggestions. If Apple expanded the feature by letting you scroll horizontally through more options, I suspect I’d use Smart Reply even more.

Have you been using iOS 27’s Smart Reply feature in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

  • Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, had links to gaming tycoons, hundreds of shell companies and an alleged Cambodian criminal group, the Financial Times reported on Saturday.
  • TNW has not independently verified either report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia’s headquarters on San Tomas Expressway in Santa Clara, California.

Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, had links to gaming tycoons, hundreds of shell companies and an alleged Cambodian criminal group, the Financial Times reported on Saturday. Together they formed a network that supplied Nvidia chips to China. A day earlier, The New York Times tied companies linked to her family to suppliers of China’s military.

TNW has not independently verified either report. US officials suspect Huang of working for Chinese intelligence, the Times first reported in October, describing a Chinese spy plot. Beijing calls the claim a smear. Jensen Huang quit as Nvidia’s chief executive on 12 November after admitting an affair with her. They are not related.

According to recent reports, the FT’s Zijing Wu and Haohsiang Ko traced the Alice Huang chip network through hundreds of filings and more than a dozen sources. Its companies made billions moving Nvidia chips into China, not necessarily aware of the full picture, the paper reported.

It started with Inspur, one of Nvidia’s largest server partners in China. The US put Inspur on its entity list in March 2023, but not its part-owned US unit. Renamed Aivres, that unit kept trading with Nvidia. Inside Nvidia there were questions over whether it should count as a partner, a person with direct knowledge told the FT. Nvidia concluded that it met all compliance and export control rules.

Some of Inspur’s Chinese clients then turned to Century Huatong, an online gaming group turned data centre investor. The answer, people familiar with the strategy remarked, was an offshore shell branded as a “neocloud”. That shell became Megaspeed, with Huang as its trusted public face.

Industry observers note that kang Wei, whom the FT calls her husband and the Times her business partner, was an early investor in Century Huatong, filings show. Megaspeed grew out of the Singapore arm of 7Road, a gaming firm that Huang and Century Huatong both backed. Its Malaysian unit, Speedmatrix, declared about $4.6bn of imports from Aivres in the year to December 2025. The FT cites ImportGenius trade data.

Sources indicate that the last step was smuggling the chips into China. Hu Xiaowei filled at least part of that role, people familiar with the matter told the FT. US authorities call Hu the “second-in-command” at Prince Group. The US Treasury has named the group a transnational criminal organisation. Hu was arrested in Japan this summer.

In a recent development, A spokesperson for the Prince group of companies said Hu never worked for the business and called the US allegations unsupported. The FT could not reach Hu.

Nvidia stated it put Megaspeed and a subsidiary on its block list in 2025 and has also restricted sales to Aivres. Megaspeed has said it runs a lawful business, and that Huang left in August 2025. Tencent, which owns 10.1% of Century Huatong, said it knew nothing of the activities. The FT found no evidence that Tencent or Alibaba took part.

The Times reviewed a confidential analysis by Strider Technologies, an intelligence firm staffed by former intelligence officers. About $3.6bn of Chinese state money flowed through companies tied to Huang’s family or associates, it found. The money funded projects including data centres with Nvidia chips. The Times remarked it confirmed many of the ties itself.

Recent findings suggest that most links are indirect, the Times mentioned, and it is unclear whether the military used any of the computing power. The paper had already reported that Megaspeed’s backer Alibaba co-founded a military-linked lab.

“Follow the money and, too often, you find the P.L.A. at the end of it,” Strider’s chief executive, Greg Levesque, told the Times.

It has been revealed that both papers point to Century Litong, a Shanghai firm founded by Century Longteng. The FT says Longteng was a venture between Century Huatong and a vehicle Huang controlled with her sister. The Times names the sister’s firm.

Industry observers note that century Litong was a key distributor of smuggled Nvidia chips in China, people with knowledge of the deals told the FT. The Information first reported its role. Its owner, Jiangsu Lettall Electronic, also controls a maker of Chinese radar and missile parts, the Times reported.

In a recent development, nvidia sought permission to sell more than 40,000 H200s to Century Litong’s Hong Kong unit, licence files released on Thursday by a House committee show. An Nvidia spokesman told the Times that, despite receiving some licences, it had already stopped shipping H200s to China, and had not and would not ship to that firm. Century Litong states it has no dealings with Huang. Nvidia’s shares, meanwhile, have had their worst run since 2008.

HomeKit Weekly: Lafaer’s 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes an annoying automation in Apple Home

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home.
  • HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.
  • Sources indicate that A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home. The only carve-out is lighting, because some rooms are hard to judge by time of day alone. Depending on the windows and placement against the sun, some rooms might need light-based automations earlier in the day than others. The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes that with a light sensor most motion sensors lack, along with mmWave radar.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Sources indicate that A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations. If you’re still for long periods, you’re invisible, and the automation assumes the room is empty. The Lafaer LWR02 pairs PIR with 2.4 GHz mmWave radar. The PIR-based motion sees you walking in, and the radar sees the minor stuff, like breathing and shifting on the couch, so the room stays “occupied” for as long as you are in it. The two together also reduce false positives from ceiling fans, curtains, and the dog, because the radar and PIR both must agree before the sensor reports motion.

In Apple Home, that demonstrates up as an occupancy sensor and a motion sensor from the same device.

“Turn on the lights when someone enters” is a common automation I use, but it can be tricky. What if you only want it when it’s not light outside? Doing it based on time of day sometimes works, but what about depending on where the windows are facing, etc.? You might have a room that gets darker an hour earlier than another room. “Turn on the lights when someone enters, and it’s dark in the room” is what the light sensor can handle for you.

It has been revealed that in the Home app, that means triggering a sensor for occupancy, then converting the automation into a Shortcut and adding a condition for the light level. It’s a few extra steps, but it does really give you more fine control over how it works.

Presence, motion, light, temperature, and humidity all come from the same device, and each one appears in Apple Home as its own sensor, so you can build automations around whichever ones fit the room.

It’s IPX3-rated, so bathrooms, kitchens, and laundry rooms are fine to use in. Coverage is about 13 feet for presence and 26 for motion across about 120 degrees, which works in a bedroom, office, or bathroom. It’s not going to cover a great room from one corner. The base is a magnetic half sphere, so you can aim it, and it mounts with adhesive or sits on a shelf. I generally like to use the shelf for these types of sensors.

Recent findings suggest that the Lafaer LWR02 is Matter over Thread, so it pairs directly with a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K with no Lafaer hub or account needed. It runs on two included AAA batteries, is rated for up to two years, and rechargeable AAAs work with it as well. Thread is why a sensor doing this much can last that long on batteries. All sensor data is processed locally, so it only uses a trickle on the batteries.

In a recent development, lights that turn off while you’re sitting still in the room are the reason a lot of people stop using motion automations in smart homes. The Lafaer LWR02 fixes that with mmWave radar and then lets you have more granular control of light-based automations based on what’s actually in the environment in the room, not just the time of day.
